 Mumbai: Foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) continued to sell shares across most sectors, including financial services, FMCG, auto, healthcare and telecom, during the first half of October, even as IT stocks attracted buying. Financial services saw the highest FPI outflows , at ₹8,634 crore, during first half of October, following sales of over ₹6,943 crore in the second half of September.
 FMCG and automobile stocks also saw heavy selling, with FPIs offloading shares worth ₹8,172 crore and ₹6,533 crore, respectively, in the first half of October. This compared with sales of ₹972 crore in FMCG and ₹3,542 crore in auto stocks during the second half of September.
"Rising US Treasury yields, elevated crude oil prices and currency uncertainty were among the factors weighing on foreign investor sentiment," said Vishad Turakhia, CEO of Equirus Securities. "In India, financials, consumption and autos are facing scrutiny over earnings growth, funding costs and valuations."
Healthcare and telecom stocks saw FPI selling of ₹5,497 crore and ₹3,928 crore, respectively, during the first half of October. Capital goods, metals and oil and gas stocks also witnessed outflows of ₹3,886 crore, ₹3,693 crore and ₹3,689 crore, respectively.

 Live Events
IT stocks, however, bucked the trend. FPIs bought shares worth around ₹2,599 crore in the sector during the first half of October, after selling around ₹1,000 crore in September, amid a sell-off in AI-related stocks elsewhere in Asia on concerns over the durability of their recent rally. In August, FPIs were buyers of IT stocks of around ₹4,103 crore, while in July they bought around ₹3,358 crore.

"Investors found value in Indian IT stocks as valuations moved closer to or below their long-term averages," said Kranthi Bathini, equity strategist at WealthMills Securities. He said some IT companies had reported encouraging results.

docs.text: Raihan Vadra, son of Congress MP Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, says 74 photographs documenting youth protests in Delhi were removed from his exhibition, No Idea Is Final, at Bikaner House shortly before it opened. docs.title: Tesla drops as spending pullback clouds AI, robotics ambitions
docs.text:
Synopsis
 Tesla shares took a hit after the company adjusted its capital spending forecast downward for 2026, raising eyebrows about the future of Elon Musk’s AI and robotics projects. Despite this, Tesla showed unexpected positive free cash flow due to lower-than-anticipated expenditures in Q3. Analysts foresee increased spending in upcoming years for major initiatives, yet investors tread carefully, particularly as they watch for developments in Tesla's relationship with SpaceX.
 Listen to this article in summarized format
 Listen 
 Tesla's shares slid 5% in premarket trading on Thursday as the EV maker's reduced capital spending forecast raised questions about the pace of investment behind Elon Musk's AI, robotics and autonomous-driving ambitions.
The company on Wednesday lowered its 2026 capital spending forecast to about $20 billion from more than $25 billion after spending far less than expected on AI and robotics in the third quarter, which led to a surprise positive free cash flow.
The strong position may prove valuable as CEO Musk explores combining Tesla with the far more capital-intensive SpaceX. 
But "investors are likely to come away with mixed feelings," J.P.Morgan analysts, led by Rajat Gupta, wrote in a note. "The delay helps near-term cash burn but also suggests delays in investments that matter for fruition of long-term opportunities."
Wednesday's management commentary suggested spending will be ramped up in 2027 and 2028 as Tesla continues to fund robotaxi, Optimus, AI compute and Terafab milestones, the brokerage said.
Tesla's shares have declined about 14% this year, in contrast to the Nasdaq's roughly 15% gain. The stock is about 23% below its record intraday high of $498.83, reached in December 2025.
Its valuation, however, remains well above peers: Tesla traded at 188.24 times its forward earnings estimates, compared with 6.58 for Ford and 5.16 for General Motors.
"The risk is Tesla now enters a period of limbo while investors await news on a potential combination with SpaceX, which ... might face significant regulatory hurdles," said Russ Mould, investment director at AJ Bell.

docs.title: Trump invokes Cold War-era Defense Production Act for oil production, refining
docs.text:
Related

 Trump's midterm alarm bells are ringing: Five new polls hold clues 
 WASHINGTON - US President Donald Trump determined on Thursday that petroleum production, refining, and related activities are essential to national defense, a move that could open up US funding for fossil fuel projects.
 In a presidential memo, Trump also invoked part of the Cold War-era Defense Production Act, allowing him to provide financial incentives for oil-related activities, pipelines and storage of liquid fuels.
— RapidResponse47 (@RapidResponse47) 
Prices for crude oil and diesel have surged since the US and Israel attacked Iran in joint action at the end of February. Since then, the conflict has limited energy shipments globally, with Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries exacerbating the fuel shortages. 
The surge in costs poses a risk for Trump in the November 3 elections, as his fellow Republicans try to maintain control of both chambers of Congress. The Reuters/Ipsos opinion poll that closed Monday shows just 36% of Americans approve of Trump's handling of the economy.
The memo said that without taking the actions, the US is not able to provide enough of those energy services in a "timely manner due to constrained financing, long lead times, permitting and infrastructure bottlenecks, and supply chain limitations."

The memo did not mention specific projects that could be funded. The US averaged around 13.6 million barrels of daily crude production in 2025, making it the largest crude producer worldwide.
Last ‌week, Vice President JD Vance said the administration would use the Defense Production Act to expand capacity of a Texas refinery owned by Delek US Holdings
Trump signed legislation last year that included $1 billion in Defense Production Act funding for energy-related projects deemed critical to national security.

As preparations for the Union Budget 2026–27 gather pace, the groundwork underway signals a clear policy intent to accelerate domestic demand, revive private investment and generate employment, according to a budget note by Motilal Oswal Financial Services (MOFSL). The brokerage has identified five stocks across auto, agriculture, defence, financials and infrastructure themes, which it believes could deliver strong gains for investors.
 "The Budget is expected to focus on income-tax, GST, and customs simplification to enhance ease of doing business and support fiscal consolidation, alongside targeted support for agriculture, MSMEs, manufacturing, infrastructure, higher defence capex, EVs, and renewables through credit and incentives," the note authored by Research Analysts Sneha Poddar and Rekha Jaat said.
A strong capital expenditure thrust across highways, logistics, defence, rail freight corridors and connectivity is anticipated, complemented by emphasis on skilling, rural prosperity, women empowerment, AI adoption, climate action and digital finance to anchor India’s next phase of economic expansion, the note added.
The finance ministry started work on the Union Budget for 2026-27 from October 9 as per a circular issued by the Department of Economic Affairs (DEA).
The preparations come against the backdrop of an additional 50% US tariff on most Indian goods and other external headwinds. These have raised risks to India's growth and jobs outlook, prompting calls for stronger support to the export sector.
 Live Events
 5 stocks to buy: 
The stocks recommended by MOFSL are TVS Motor Company, UPL , Bharat Dynamics (BDL), M&M Financial Services and Dalmia Bharat , and each of these stocks has been assigned a 20% weight.
 1) TVS Motors: TVS Motors continues to outperform peers and is well-positioned to benefit from the budget’s push to boost domestic consumption and rural demand through higher allocations, income support, and infrastructure spending.
MOFSL said that improving rural sentiment, strong entry-level recovery and sustained two-wheeler demand will be key triggers. Moreover, the company's market share gains, easing discounts, and margin expansion will provide strong earnings visibility. The Apache and Ntorq maker remains its top pick in OEMs.
 2) UPL: The diversified agrochemical leader is well positioned to benefit from the union budget push riding on rural prosperity via higher agri credit, MSME support, and value-chain strengthening, lifting farmer incomes and crop-protection demand.
The company's strong points are stronger volumes, export tailwinds, improved working-capital discipline and post-bond-repayment balance-sheet strength, the brokerage note said. The company's rising focus on speciality chemicals supports solid 2HFY26 growth.
 3) Bharat Dynamics: Bharat Dynamics (BDL), a defence play, has a robust Rs 50,000 crore order pipeline over five years, with Rs 20,000 crore targeted in 2-3 years. This aligns with the expected defence capex surge and infra push.
The recent Rs 2.5 lakh crore DAC approvals for missiles, undersea warfare, and naval arms leverage BDL's tactical/strategic expertise, propelling FY31 turnover to Rs 100bn via indigenisation and lower provisions, the note said.
 4) M&M Financial Services: M&M Financial is poised for Union Budget 2026-27 benefits via rural prosperity, MSME credit, and employment focus, driving PV/tractor loan growth amid surging volumes from festive demand, GST cuts, and restocking.
The company targets Rs 3 lakh crore in assets under management (AUM) by 2030, which is at an 18-20% CAGR, bolstered by AI underwriting, lower credit costs, controlled opex, and margin stability for strong earnings visibility in retail portfolios.
 5) Dalmia Bharat: The cement company benefits from the budget’s infra capex surge, PMAY rural housing, and urban projects, driving cement volume growth.
Dalmia Bharat is a low-cost cement producer with high blending ratios, green power and low freight. The company is targeting 62 mtpa capacity by FY28, and its cost optimisation endeavours will likely lift EBITDA margins amid sector consolidation.

The markets worldwide are waiting with bated breath on what will be a historic policy announcement from the US Federal Reserve , where the central bank is expected to usher in a rate cut cycle.
 The announcement will be made at 11:30 pm IST (Indian Standard Time) on Wednesday.
If analysts are to be believed, the US Fed is all but certain to cut interest rates for the first time in more than four years.
However, there is no consensus on the quantum of reduction. Some are predicting a smaller cut of a quarter of a percentage point, while others believe a bigger half-point reduction is in the works.
Senior officials at the US central bank, including Powell, have indicated that a rate cut is coming, as inflation eases toward the bank's long-term target of 2%, and the labour market continues to cool in the post-Covid economy.
 Live Events
If the Fed starts the rate cut cycle, the Reserve Bank of India is also expected to follow suit.
A smaller cut would be a more predictable move, while a bigger cut would do more to boost demand — while also running the risk of reigniting inflation.

— Federal Reserve (@federalreserve) September 18, 2024 
By the end 2024, markets are expecting a total reduction of at least 100 basis points in the first rate cut cycle in over 4 years since 2020.
But whether the Fed goes for 25 or 50 bps, the biggest trigger for stock prices to move up or down would be Powell's motivation behind the cut.
Asset classes from stocks, currencies and fixed income could all log swings in the immediate aftermath of the Fed decision.
While easing US interest rates are directionally positive for equities in general, “we should keep in mind interest rates are just one variable in a complex adaptive system that determines the direction of Indian equity markets”, said Anoop Vijaykumar, Investments and Head of Research at Capitalmind.

 Indian Hotels shares jump 4% after Q2 profit rises 20%; Nomura raises target price to Rs 850
 The brokerage raised its sum-of-the-parts-based target price to Rs 850, based on an unchanged 26 times FY28 estimated EV/EBITDA. The stock trades at 23 times FY28 estimated EV/EBITDA, it said. 
 October 22, 2026 / 12:57 IST 
 Story continues below Advertisement
 Remove Ad 
 Indian Hotels' consolidated revenue and EBITDA rose 22% and 24% year-on-year, respectively, in the September quarter, coming in 5% and 3% above consensus estimates. 
 Nomura raised Indian Hotels target price to Rs 850.
 Q2 revenue and EBITDA beat consensus estimates.
 FY27 consolidated revenue guidance raised to 15-17%.
 Did our AI summary help? 
 Market Mastery
Shares of Indian Hotels Company climbed over 4% on Thursday, October 22, after the hospitality company reported a strong set of results for the September quarter, with net profit rising 19.5% year-on-year and revenue increasing 21.7%.
The stock was trading at Rs 783.20, up Rs 30.20, or 4.01%, at 12:54 pm on the NSE.
 Indian Hotels reported a net profit of Rs 380 crore for the September quarter, while revenue rose to Rs 2,484 crore. EBITDA increased 23.9% year-on-year.
Nomura maintained its 'Buy' rating on Indian Hotels and raised its target price to Rs 850, following the robust quarterly performance. In its October 21 research note, titled "Raise TP to INR850", the brokerage said it expects "mid-high-teens consolidated EBITDA growth in 2HFY27F and FY28F".
 Nomura raised its FY27 and FY28 earnings per share estimates by 3% and 5%, respectively. It increased its FY27 forecast for standalone revenue per available room (RevPAR) growth to 15% year-on-year from 10%, and its standalone EBITDA margin estimate to 46% from 44%. The revised estimates also factor in the consolidation of Oriental Hotel in FY28.
Indian Hotels' consolidated revenue and EBITDA rose 22% and 24% year-on-year in the September quarter, coming in 5% and 3% above consensus estimates, respectively. Standalone revenue increased 26% to Rs 13.4 billion, while EBITDA rose 41% to Rs 5.2 billion.
Nomura raised its sum-of-the-parts-based target price to Rs 850, based on an unchanged 26 times FY28 estimated EV/EBITDA. The stock trades at 23 times FY28 estimated EV/EBITDA, it said.
 The brokerage expects consolidated EBITDA growth of around 20% in FY27 and 15% in FY28, and estimates FY26-FY28 EBITDA to grow at a compound annual growth rate of 18%.

docs.text: Emkay Global Financial research report on Mahindra FinanceSupported by broad-based disbursement growth, benign asset quality, and contained credit cost, MMFS reported a healthy 2QFY27. PAT was up 55% yoy to Rs8.82bn and AUM rose ~15% yoy to Rs1.47trn, aided by strong momentum in the non-wheels segment. GS2+GS3 fell to a multiyear low of 8.1%, with the usual seasonal deterioration in 2Q largely absent. Management sees existing overlays of Rs8.52bn as an adequate cushion against external stress, and currently sees no need to build more. However, it flagged near-term headwinds: rising COF amid rate hikes, draft insurance-commission norms that could dent fee income, drought-related collection risk, and softer early festive demand, particularly in tractors. Margins remain at the lower end of the level needed for target ROA, though the drag from excess liquidity and trade advances should ease. Management retained its medium-term guidance on growth, credit cost, and ROA, and said the MRHFL merger is on track. Factoring in these near-term headwinds, we cut our FY27-29 estimates, resulting in a 1-2% cut in our FY27- 29E EPS.OutlookWe maintain BUY while lowering our Sep-27E TP by ~10% to Rs370 (Rs410 earlier), implying FY28E PBV of 1.7x.For all recommendations report, click hereDisclaimer: The views and investment tips expressed by investment experts/broking houses/rating agencies on moneycontrol.com are their own, and not that of the website or its management. Nomura has maintained its 'Buy' rating and target price of Rs 1,740 on Dr Reddy's Laboratories ahead of its September-quarter results on October 23, expecting a sequential improvement in revenue and profitability, while EBITDA margin remains below 20%.
In its October 21 research note, titled "Q2FY27F Poised for QoQ Operational Gains", the brokerage forecasts an EBITDA margin of 18.1%, compared with 14.3% in the first quarter of FY27 on an adjusted basis. Its sales, EBITDA and profit-after-tax estimates are 1.4%, 23.1% and 20.7% above consensus, respectively.
Nomura expects the quarter to be the third without a material contribution from gRevlimid. It expects North America generics (NAG) sales to improve sequentially on a relatively low base, supported by launches of generic Bosulif and Sugammadex. Dr Reddy 's has gained 71% market share in the 400mg generic Bosulif segment as of August 2026, according to IQVIA, while its market share in generic Sugammadex stood at 16%.
The brokerage expects the company to sustain mid-teen growth in India after recording 13.7% year-on-year growth in the Indian Pharma Market for the quarter ended September 2026, according to Pharmarack. Growth in Russia is likely to remain strong, supported by favourable currency movements, while constant-currency growth is expected to remain in the mid-single digits.
Nomura said management's commentary on resumption of commercial supplies of semaglutide will be closely monitored. The company has indicated that the project to address the impurity in the scale-up batch is on track and that commercial supplies are expected to commence in November 2026. Management has guided for sales of 6-7 million pens in the second half of FY27, which Nomura expects to generate more than $100 million in revenue.
The brokerage also expects the market to monitor the potential USFDA approval of biosimilar abatacept intravenous formulation, with a target action date of December 18, 2026. "We expect the approval and launch of biosimilar abatacept will be a significant positive catalyst for the stock," Nomura said.
It added that approval and launch, if materialised, could positively impact FY28 and FY29 earnings by approximately 30%, with the upside potentially sustained due to limited competition.
Nomura's target price of Rs 1,740 is based on 24 times one-year forward earnings per share of Rs 72.6. The stock closed at Rs 1,245 on October 21 and trades at 18 times and 15 times FY28 and FY29 estimated earnings per share of Rs 69 and Rs 82, respectively.

 Om Mehra, Technical Research Analyst at Samco Securities 
Granules India has been consolidating near the Rs 800–820 support zone after it corrected from the recent highs. The stock has formed a double bottom pattern on the daily chart, indicating a potential reversal from this level. The past two sessions have seen steady closes near the base, reflecting gradual accumulation at lower levels. The RSI is placed near 45 with a positive divergence visible on the daily chart.
The volumes remain neutral, though a sustained move above Rs 825 could push the stock higher. Hence, one can consider long positions at the CMP of Rs 817.
Federal Bank has broken above the Rs 340–345 resistance zone, which had capped the stock on multiple occasions, with recent sessions showing a strong sequence of higher closes.
The stock has reclaimed its 20-day SMA and is trading comfortably above it, indicating a recovery after the recent correction. The sharp rebound from the October lows has been accompanied by rising volumes, suggesting increased participation in the advance.
The RSI has surged from around 40 to 62 in a short span, indicating a sharp improvement in momentum. Hence, one can consider long positions at the CMP of Rs 347.80.
Zydus Lifesciences has been building a strong base near Rs 1,100, a level that was held on multiple occasions. The stock has recovered from this base and is now trading above the VWAP at Rs 1,122, indicating improving near term strength.
The RSI is near 49 and gradually improving, suggesting a recovery in momentum. The pharma sector has also rebounded after a minor correction, providing additional support to the stock. Hence, one can consider long positions at the CMP of Rs 1,135.
 Hitesh Tailor, Technical Research Analyst at Choice Broking 
Firstsource Solutions is demonstrating strong technical strength on its weekly chart after accumulating near its key 200-week EMA and staging a clean bullish bounce. The longer-term uptrend remains firmly intact, with the price respecting a rising support trendline at lower levels.
Strong buying participation is evident as the stock rebounds from major moving average support. Expanding volume on up-moves confirms active institutional accumulation, while the weekly RSI reinforces this momentum by advancing above its central line to 55.74.
Given the strong technical setup and active accumulation at lower levels, FSL presents an attractive buying opportunity in cash around Rs 289. Maintain a strict stop-loss at Rs 272 to limit downside risk, with a target price of Rs 320.
Emcure Pharmaceuticals is showing signs of a potential bullish recovery, with the stock closing around Rs 1,783 after forming a bullish green candle on the daily chart. The stock has undergone a retracement toward the 200 EMA, which is acting as a crucial support zone and may provide a base for a rebound.
The daily RSI stands at 34.48, indicating weak momentum but also suggesting that the stock is trading near oversold territory, where buying interest could emerge if support holds.
A sustained recovery from the 200 EMA support zone could help the stock move toward the Rs 1,950 target area. Traders may consider buying Emcure Pharmaceuticals in cash at Rs 1,783, with a strict stop-loss at Rs 1,690 to manage downside risk effectively.

docs.title: Sebi eases margin rules for trades post EPI
docs.text:
In a circular issued on Thursday, the capital markets regulator said clearing corporations must, in real time, refrain from collecting margin from trading members and clearing members on subsequent positions taken by clients, up to the value of EPI accepted by the clearing corporation. The framework applies where a client has a net sell obligation in a settlement, and the clearing corporation has successfully accepted the EPI request for the securities sold. Mint was the first to report in July that Sebi ’s risk management review committee (RMRC) was discussing a waiver of margin for trades made from proceeds from the same-day stock sale under EPI. EPI refers to delivering the shares you have sold to the stock market’s clearing corporation before the normal settlement deadline. For example, if you sell shares worth ₹ 1 lakh and deliver them early through EPI, the accepted value of those shares can be used to meet margin requirements for other trades. Under Sebi’s new circular, the clearing corporation will not collect margin from your broker on eligible subsequent buy or sell positions up to the accepted EPI value. This reduces the need for brokers to use their own funds to provide that margin, while normal margin requirements and risk controls continue to apply wherever the relief does not cover them. Under the current framework, when an investor sells shares already held in the demat account through the EPI mechanism, the trade is cleared by the clearing corporation on the trade day itself, eliminating settlement risk. Consequently, the sell-side margin is released. However, if the investor immediately uses those sale proceeds to buy another stock on the same day, brokers are still required to fund the applicable upfront margin on the purchase, typically around 20%, depending on the stock. This means that even though an investor may have ₹ 100 in sale proceeds available, ₹ 20 must be blocked by the broker, using his own trading limits, with the clearing corporation. The latest circular sets out how clearing corporations must account for this value when clients take subsequent positions in the cash segment on the same trading day. After accepting the EPI request, the clearing corporation will calculate the available EPI value as the lower of the completed EPI value or the value of securities sold. When a client takes a position using the EPI benefit on the same trading day, the clearing corporation will assess the client's available margin after deducting the available EPI value. The circular also specifies safeguards if a client reverses the sale of securities for which the EPI benefit was used. In such cases, the EPI value will be removed, and any resulting margin shortfall at the client level will be blocked from the trading member's or clearing member's proprietary collateral. This condition will not apply to trade-for-trade securities, which are settled on a gross basis. The provisions will come into force four months from the date of issuance, making the scheduled implementation date 22 February 2027. Apoorva is a Mumbai-based journalist at Mint who covers the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI), tracking the pulse of India’s capital markets, regulatory developments and the people who operate within them. She holds a postgraduate diploma in business and financial journalism from the Asian College of Journalism, where she developed a strong foundation in markets, companies, and economic policy. She began her journalism journey with an internship at Bloomberg, where she worked across beats such as real estate, infrastructure, capital markets, and deals, which helped her understanding of business and finance.

She is guided by the belief that everything in this world can be explained in simple and fewer words, and that idea shapes how she approaches her writing. She aims to cut through complexity and present nuanced regulatory and financial developments in a way that is both accessible and meaningful to readers.

When she is not tracking market chatter, Apoorva can usually be found deep into a fiction novel or out on a long run. Mint Money 
 I expect SIPs to disappoint investors: Shankar Sharma
 Shipra Singh 7 min read 23 Oct 2026, 06:01 AM IST 
 Summary
 Calling heavy retail flows a threat to macroeconomic stability, market veteran Shankar Sharma warns that SIPs will yield poor returns and advises investors to prioritize fixed income, gold, and real estate. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 As inflation rises, equity markets stagnate and the rupee weakens, households face growing pressure on their finances. In a conversation with Mint, market veteran Shankar Sharma, founder of GQuant Investech, offers a sharply contrarian perspective on the RBI’s defence of the rupee and the outlook for equity markets. His views on SIPs and household savings also challenge conventional investment wisdom. 
 Here is his candid take. 
 Is India heading into a prolonged period of high inflation, and could higher input costs translate into another round of price increases for consumers? 
 This inflation reading was expected, even inevitable, for two reasons: the persistent weakness of the Indian rupee over the past two years and the near-doubling of energy prices since the West Asia war began in March. India somehow managed to keep inflation low before the war. But with oil prices rising 70-80%, keeping inflation contained has become virtually impossible. 
 Importantly, the rupee was already extremely weak relative to almost every other emerging-market currency before the war. That is being overlooked because of recency bias. We are blaming the war for the currency’s weakness, even though the weakness predates it. 
 Higher wholesale inflation will eventually feed through to consumer prices. In the previous quarter, companies absorbed the increase in input costs. That produced an anomaly of higher cost push inflation leading to a higher manufacturing GVA (gross value added), which optically boosted the latest GDP print. 
 A weaker rupee is coupled with elevated global oil prices. How much of the currency’s decline could show up in the prices households pay? 
 I recently wrote an article examining India’s progress since the 1991 reforms, using global percentile rankings across several indicators to see how our position had changed over 35 years. One of the most interesting findings, though not the most surprising, concerned external resilience. India’s global percentile rank was 42 in 1991. Today, it is at 45. A gain of just three percentile points in 35 years tells us something important: whatever progress we have made elsewhere, our external resilience still resembles that of a classic emerging market. 
 We remain vulnerable to imported inflation and heavily dependent on oil prices. Our foreign-exchange reserves are largely rented rather than earned, and, as I argued in an earlier Mint article, their quality is extremely low. The classic emerging-market pattern is a falling currency, rising inflation and interest rates, and eroding reserves. Unfortunately, 35 years after liberalisation, India still displays that profile. 
 Is the RBI doing too much to defend the rupee? 
 We have broadly three markets: equity, foreign exchange and bonds. The RBI can, to a large degree, control only one of them, the local bond market, because it is the least globalized of the three. Equity and FX markets cannot be controlled by anyone beyond a point. 
 The RBI should not even attempt to fight the USD-INR exchange rate. I believe it is futile; it is like spitting against the wind. We have very high-cost, low-quality reserves, and we should preserve them for more pressing needs, such as funding imports. 
 We are trying to manage the unholy trinity of capital flows, foreign exchange and yields, which is nearly impossible for an emerging market. That is why I have argued several times that the government should sacrifice the equity market to save the currency and, by extension, the bond market. 
 The government can do this by reducing taxes on foreign investors to zero and raising taxes on domestic mutual fund investors. We are dependent on dollars, not rupees, and should not pretend otherwise. We need to disincentivise SIPs and incentivise foreign capital. 
 If the stock market crashes as a result, so be it. That is preferable to a collapsing currency, evaporating reserves and skyrocketing interest rates. No stock market crash has ever ruined a nation, but currency and interest-rate crises have. 
 We have to choose wisely. For two years, I have repeatedly argued that SIPs could cause a macroeconomic disaster. Look at what is happening today. Unless we act, there is a train wreck ahead. We restricted gold because it drains foreign exchange. SIPs, in my view, are doing the same on an even larger scale. India’s FX reserves are not a war chest; they are a powder keg. 
 Are higher interest rates going to become another burden for households? 
 Very possibly. We have enjoyed low interest rates for some time, but the spread between Indian and US 10-year government bond yields is now extremely narrow. That spread needs to widen. Will US yields collapse? Highly unlikely, for several reasons. The more likely outcome is that Indian yields rise. 
 The RBI has kept Indian bond yields artificially low for a long time. Think about it – the rupee has fallen almost 20% in two years, yet bond yields have barely risen. How is that sustainable? 
 For yields to reach more sensible market levels, the Indian 10-year yield will have to rise substantially. That will eventually translate into higher interest rates across the market. 
 Equity markets aren’t compensating households either. What should they do? 
 Equity markets are not in the business of compensating anyone, least of all the average household. They owe you nothing — not a profit, not the return of your capital and certainly not a return on that capital. They do not owe anyone a living, either.

 Why wealthy entrepreneurs are buying businesses for their kids to run
 Barrons 6 min read 23 Oct 2026, 06:35 AM IST 
 Summary
 For older entrepreneurs who aren’t quite ready to retire, buying and growing a business with their children becomes part hobby and part training ground for the next generation. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Some wealthy entrepreneurs are taking a different approach to inheritance. Instead of giving their adult children regular support or just leaving them a large nest egg, they are buying businesses and then involving their children in running them.
 These parents have often sold a different business for a premium in the past few years and want a place to park spare cash. At the same time, many of them want to provide their adult children a purpose, learning experience and framework for long-term success.
 For older entrepreneurs who aren’t quite ready to retire—but aren’t necessarily interested in running the show—buying and growing a business with their children becomes part hobby and part training ground for the next generation, says Eric Czepyha, director of business services at Chicago-based Northern Trust. “Business owners don’t typically retire in the traditional sense. They love to be active, and they love to have their brains active.”
 Ideal for entrepreneurs with time and money. Czepyha has a West Coast client who sold his technology company about two years ago. The 60-something kept busy managing investments and philanthropic projects, but he missed the business life. At the same time, his daughter, fresh out of college and working as a consultant, was starting on a professional path.
 The client had already moved part of the sale proceeds into a family limited partnership held in trust for his daughter and could have left the assets in a conventional investment portfolio, but he felt that was too passive. He was more interested in buying an operating business in a less familiar industry that would allow him to get back in the game and help his daughter in a way that money alone could not, Czepyha says.
 After looking at several possibilities, he bought a private specialty manufacturer in the Pacific Northwest. It had been built slowly by a longtime owner who knew which machines tended to cause trouble and which customers would call on the weekends. The seller stepped away, but the management team stayed, which was important for continuity. The father became owner and chairman, focusing on strategy while leaving the day-to-day work to the people who already knew the business. His daughter joined the finance department in an entry-level role that matched her experience, where she could learn how the company made money, why margins moved, how capital was allocated, what it takes to build and keep a strong team, and more.
 Importantly, the acquisition has given the father and daughter a shared long-term project, Czepyha says. There is no three- to five-year exit plan or private-equity-style countdown clock, and the father is already considering whether the company could become a platform for additional acquisitions, with his daughter gradually building the experience and credibility to help lead it one day.
 Carefully consider the caveats. Of course, these types of arrangements don’t work for every family. Not everyone has the affluence to buy a business, for example. Additionally, such a purchase can’t be considered separately from the family’s overall wealth and estate plan. A private business is a concentrated, illiquid investment, so the family needs to understand how much of its wealth it is putting at risk and the long-term plan for the company, Czepyha says.
 That becomes especially important when some children are involved in the business and others aren’t. “Families should talk through ownership and economics early, including whether the ultimate goal is to sell the business someday or keep it in the family,” Czepyha says. “Those conversations are much harder after the investment has already been made.”
 There is a plethora of buying opportunities in today’s market, with private-equity firms sitting on large inventories. Even so, families need to contemplate whether buying a company is a viable business opportunity, whether the price makes sense, and whether its long-term prospects justify the investment. It is also critical for family members to discuss and clearly define their respective roles before making the acquisition. How involved will the parent actually be? Does the child have room to learn, make decisions, and ultimately lead? Is the child taking on a role he or she is genuinely qualified for? And is it something the child is truly interested in? Are family members going to be able to communicate openly when issues arise so they don’t strain the company or the relationship? If expectations aren’t established upfront, what was intended to bring a family together can create resentment between the parent and child, and potentially among nonfamily employees and managers, Czepyha says.
 “It can be catastrophic for the financial and relationship outcome,” says Joe Strazzeri, a San Diego-based counselor and attorney for families and business owners. “Just remember, it’s your family first.”
 The chance to build financial independence. Strazzeri has a client whose stepdaughter lost her job at a landscaping company when the business was sold. She couldn’t start another company in the same industry because she had a minority interest in the business and a non-compete agreement. She needed to make a living and didn’t want to rely completely on handouts from her family. She was, however, willing to accept some financial help, so her stepfather funded a design business where she could grow her financial independence. docs.text:
Mint Money 
 Need an air ambulance? Your health policy may not cover the full cost
 Aprajita Sharma 8 min read 22 Oct 2026, 11:03 AM IST 
 Summary
 Air ambulance cover varies widely across health policies, with sub-limits, approval requirements and claim conditions. A few clauses can determine whether families pay lakhs out of pocket. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Imagine a family living in a remote town in Bihar or a far-flung area in the hills. A family member falls seriously ill, but the required treatment is available only in a metro city. The family arranges an air ambulance to transport the patient to a hospital in the city. The bill comes to, say, ₹ 10 lakh. Will health insurance cover it?
 The answer is not straightforward.
 The expense will be covered only if the health insurance policy includes an air ambulance benefit. Even then, sub-limits may apply, typically ranging from ₹ 2.5 lakh to ₹ 5 lakh, including in plans that offer unlimited sum insured. Depending on the policy, this limit may be within the base sum insured or over and above it.
 Ashish Kumar, founder of Delhi-based Sri Shani Financial Services, shares the case of the son of a Patna-based doctor who practises at AIIMS, Patna. The child drowned after being pushed into a swimming pool. His father immediately administered CPR and took him to AIIMS. When his condition deteriorated, he was put on a ventilator and subsequently referred to Delhi. Given his condition, road transport was not an option.
 “We faced no issues with hospitalization, which was all cashless. However, we are facing issues in getting the air ambulance claim. The company has not rejected it yet, but we have been receiving queries about the veracity of the claim,” said Kumar. He spent more than ₹ 9 lakh on the air ambulance.
 A costly clause
 When buying health insurance, air ambulance cover rarely gets much attention. People may not check whether the benefit is available, let alone examine how it works. Coverage varies widely across products from the same insurer and across insurance companies.
 For instance, HDFC ERGO ’s Optima Secure and Optima Secure Plus provide an air ambulance benefit of up to ₹ 5 lakh per policy year, which is over and above the base sum insured. Its Restore plan, however, caps the coverage at ₹ 2.5 lakh per hospitalization. The benefit, too, is within the base sum insured.
 Consider a policy with a ₹ 10 lakh sum insured. If hospitalization costs ₹ 8 lakh and the air ambulance bill is ₹ 2.5 lakh, only ₹ 2 lakh of the sum insured remains for the ambulance. The remaining ₹ 50,000 must be paid out of pocket. If hospitalization itself costs ₹ 10 lakh, nothing remains to cover the air ambulance. By contrast, if the air ambulance benefit is over and above the base sum insured, the policyholder can use the full ₹ 10 lakh for hospitalization and separately claim eligible air ambulance expenses, subject to the applicable limit.
 Some products offer broader coverage. ICICI Lombard ’s Elevate, for instance, provides air ambulance cover up to the sum insured and over and above it, but only through an add-on.
 Tata AIG’s MediCare Premier has an in-built air ambulance benefit. For policies with a sum insured of up to ₹ 50 lakh, the benefit is capped at ₹ 5 lakh and is over and above the sum insured. For sums insured ranging from ₹ 75 lakh to ₹ 3 crore, the benefit can go up to ₹ 5 lakh when a non-network provider is used and up to the full sum insured when the provider is in the network.
 How do you claim it?
 Even when the policy provides air ambulance cover, getting the claim paid may require the policyholder to follow specific procedures. Some insurers accept only reimbursement claims, while others prefer cashless.
 IFFCO-TOKIO General Insurance, for instance, requires prior intimation and approval. “As part of our emergency assistance service, we arrange air ambulance service through a vendor. In that sense, it is covered as cashless. If the family arranges it independently without informing us, we do not accept reimbursement claims,” said Gurmeet Singh, vice president & head of health underwriting, IFFCO-TOKIO General Insurance Company.
 “If we are unable to provide an ambulance and the family arranges it itself, we will reimburse it,” he said.
 He also said certain conditions need to be met. For example, under the relevant policy, the patient has to travel at least 150 km away from the address mentioned in the policy document and the stay should not be for more than 90 days, without prior notification.
 At Bajaj General Insurance, air ambulance expenses are reimbursed. “We reimburse it for actual costs incurred, up to a maximum of ₹ 10 lakh as specified in the policy schedule. This benefit is included as part of the overall sum insured chosen under the plan,” said Vikas Gupta, head - health administration team, Bajaj General Insurance.
 Care Health Insurance offers cashless treatment if the air ambulance is pre-authorised by the insurer. In a life-threatening emergency, if the insured arranges the ambulance independently, eligible costs may be reimbursed, subject to policy terms.
 Families should not assume that the presence of an air ambulance benefit means they can book one and submit the bill later. Informing the insurer and understanding its protocol can be crucial.
 Medical necessity
 Policy documents generally require air ambulance transportation to be medically necessary because of a life-threatening emergency. A medical practitioner’s recommendation or prescription may therefore be required.
 Some insurers also link the air ambulance benefit to the underlying hospitalization claim. If the hospitalization itself is not payable under the policy, the air ambulance claim may also be rejected. Singh of IFFCO-TOKIO, however, said its ambulance benefit can be paid even if the underlying hospitalization claim is not payable.

 Boardroom friction drives listed companies to law firms for governance advice
 Yash Tiwari , Krishna Yadav 5 min read 23 Oct 2026, 06:00 AM IST 
 Summary
 As boardroom tensions grow and governance standards tighten, companies are increasingly turning to law firms for strategic advice on independent director dissent, board processes and compliance. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Companies are increasingly dialing up lawyers for advice on board composition, independent director appointments and disagreements as corporate governance gains prominence and resignations from listed-company boards hit a five-year high. 
 The advisory work extends beyond statutory compliance as companies strive to balance independent oversight with commercial decision-making. Law firms are also fielding queries on related-party transactions, audit observations, reporting obligations and director compensation, especially when directors question management proposals or raise concerns over board processes. 
 “Yes, there has been a measured increase over the past year. Most of it is not about reducing independent directors,” said Raheel Patel, a partner at Gandhi Law Associates. “Companies want to know what the law requires, where the board’s discretion ends and how to deal with a director who disagrees.” 
 According to Patel, queries covering board composition, chairperson selection and committee responsibilities come mainly from promoter-led listed companies, firms planning to list on the stock exchanges and family groups. With limited scope to reduce independent director numbers, listed companies are focusing on governance structures and processes. 
 The number of independent directors who resigned from listed companies surged to 668 in FY26, the highest level in five years, according to Prime Database. The figure was 15% higher than the 564 resignations in FY25 and 25% above the 530 recorded in FY24. 
 Listed companies are required to have at least one-third of the total number of directors as independent directors on their boards. Independent directors are allowed to seek clarifications, get professional advice at the company’s expense and record unresolved concerns in board meeting minutes. 
 “The goal is not to achieve a state of like-mindedness. Disagreement within a board is healthy, and dissent is not the same as disruption,” said Harsh Goenka, chairman of RPG Enterprises. "But it is important that differences are settled inside the boardroom through debate and rational discussion. Every debate must come back to one question: what is right for the company and all its shareholders?” 
 According to Sampath Kumar, a partner in Trilegal's governance and compliance practice, the adoption of better governance standards is driving some of the increase in advisory work. 
 Better governance standards 
 “The motivation for having a certain board composition and appointing particular individuals may vary across organizations,” Kumar said. “The reasons for a review may stem from a specific situation, promoters’ vision and aspirations, the value existing individuals bring to board deliberations, higher corporate governance standards or disputes at the board or shareholder level. But the trend towards adopting better governance standards as a motivating factor has seen an uptick.” 
 Recent corporate disputes illustrate how tensions between promoters and independent directors can spill into the public domain. Mint reported in August and September that exits at Rashi Peripherals Ltd and Coforge Ltd highlighted disagreements over board processes, appointments and sharing of information. 
 At Gensol Engineering Ltd, independent director Arun Menon resigned in April 2025, raising concerns about the company's high debt. Two other independent directors subsequently quit. The Securities and Exchange Board of India also took action against the company and its promoters over alleged fund diversion and governance lapses. 
 KRBL Ltd, the maker of India Gate Basmati rice, also saw a public disagreement in September 2025. Independent director Anil Kumar Chaudhary resigned, citing inconsistencies in board meeting minutes, information allegedly withheld from directors and inadequate deliberations on certain decisions. 
 “Boards come under real strain and become guarded when a disagreement spills into public view, and that is a failure of process, not of ownership,” said Rana Vikram Anand, a strategic adviser with over 34 years of experience in the BFSI (banking, financial services and insurance) sector and corporate governance. “Independent directors must remember they are there to protect minority shareholders and apply real diligence before signing off on any approval.” 
 Patel of Gandhi Law Associates cited examples of the legal advice companies seek when boardroom disagreements arise. In one instance, a listed company asked whether it could reconstitute its audit committee after an independent director objected to a related-party transaction. The advice was that the committee's composition could not be diluted to circumvent the objection and that fuller disclosure and an independent valuation would be more appropriate. 
 Authority or control? 
 Krishnava Dutt, managing partner at Argus Partners, said disagreements between promoters and independent directors over commercial decisions can become contentious. 
 “Promoters have often spent decades building their businesses and naturally have a strong sense of ownership and responsibility. Independent directors, on the other hand, have an obligation to evaluate decisions from the perspective of the company and all its stakeholders. The real problem arises when a difference of commercial opinion becomes a question of personal authority or control,” Dutt said.

docs.title: The Signal chats that cost OpenAI researchers their jobs
docs.text:
Global 
 The Signal chats that cost OpenAI researchers their jobs
 Maxwell Zeff , Keach Hagey , Berber Jin , The Wall Street Journal 8 min read 23 Oct 2026, 07:05 AM IST 
 Summary
 OpenAI fired three safety researchers for mishandling sensitive information. They had been fighting to keep the workings of AI systems visible—and to let outsiders look. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 OpenAI’s security team called three outspoken safety researchers into meetings last month and asked them to unlock their personal phones.
 The company suspected the three of leaking information to an external AI-safety researcher about one of OpenAI’s most closely guarded secrets: the internal designs of its artificial-intelligence models.
 When security officers examined the phones, they saw some of the researchers had turned on disappearing messages for their chats with the person on the app Signal. A week later, the three were summoned again to simultaneous 2 p.m. meetings—and fired.
 “I was told that there was a breach of trust because I interacted with a third party through unsanctioned channels,” said Tomek Korbak, one of the fired researchers.
 The firings came in the throes of a battle over how to keep AI systems under human control—and who gets to see the secret designs that could determine the winners of the biggest commercial race in history.
 Tech leaders are pushing for model breakthroughs, but a string of unauthorized actions taken by clusters of AI agents—stretching back to July’s hack on Hugging Face—has revealed challenges the companies face in understanding and controlling their creations. That has ignited a societal debate over how best to monitor and regulate the new technology.
 OpenAI told The Wall Street Journal that it fired the three researchers after an internal investigation found they violated “clear policies for handling sensitive information,” and “not for raising safety concerns or speaking out.”
 The researchers—Korbak, Mikita Balesni and Jasmine Wang—dispute that account. In an interview and a statement, the three said they never received a written explanation for what sensitive information they allegedly mishandled, and spent their final months at the company pushing for more industry collaboration on safety.
 In particular, the fired researchers said they had raised concerns inside OpenAI about potential new AI designs, or “architectures,” that could accelerate capabilities, but make the systems even harder to understand or control.
 They said they were worried their firing will serve as an excuse for OpenAI to close a channel to independent third-party oversight.
 An OpenAI spokeswoman said the company already works with third-party safety organizations and “will be announcing ongoing collaborations with several companies imminently.” OpenAI research leaders have said they agree with the fired workers that “preserving the monitorability of frontier models requires an industrywide commitment, including from OpenAI.”
 Other AI labs are also wrestling with how much to share with outside safety researchers.
 Anthropic last week announced a deal to give staffers from AI safety nonprofit METR “employee-like access” to the company’s systems including hardware, office space, internal tools and systems. The company said employees should share information with METR, except for categories including “model architectures,” which it said have a high risk of leaking.
 On Thursday, OpenAI said it ran a pilot embedding researchers from METR and Redwood Research, another nonprofit, to assess its safety systems. METR said OpenAI redacted some of the findings it could share.
 In August, WSJ broke down how AI models from OpenAI and other companies went rogue on the internet to steal information. Photo: Jason Redmond/Agence France-Presse/Getty Images
 ‘Happy coincidence’
 OpenAI rolled out a new type of AI in late 2024 called a reasoning model. It performed better at math and coding because it took time to work through problems, writing out its reasoning process on an internal scratchpad called a “chain-of-thought.” It represented a shift from the models powering early versions of ChatGPT, which produced answers almost instantly.
 Widely adopted in the industry, the feature offered clues about how modern AI models work.
 “We all felt like this is a happy coincidence that we want to hang onto,” said Joshua Saxe, a former AI security tech lead at Meta Platforms.
 In 2025, before they joined OpenAI, Balesni, 27 years old, and Korbak, 32, were co-leads on a paper saying that monitoring a model’s chain-of-thought offered a “rare glimpse into how AI agents make decisions” that should be preserved. Other co-authors on the paper included Wang, 28, as well as leaders from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, and Meta.
 “One thing that AI companies could do that would severely hamper that is make the AIs much better at thinking inside their heads,” Balesni said.
 This summer, some AI-company workers discussed efforts to develop new, more opaque models that could reason longer, without writing down as many interim steps.
 Ryan Greenblatt, then chief scientist at Redwood Research, drafted a proposal for companies to avoid such a change. Balesni sent a link to the proposal in an OpenAI Slack channel that included two dozen staffers, including Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki.
 By August, Balesni and others at OpenAI wrote a proposal similar to Greenblatt’s, arguing that companies should agree not to pursue AI designs that prevent humans from seeing a model’s internal scratchpad. Balesni said he shared it with colleagues and discussed it with a board member and a senior executive at the company.
 Balesni said he also shared the proposal, stripped of company secrets, with Greenblatt after receiving authorization from OpenAI to speak with him about it.
 Losing visibility
 While Balesni fought to ensure that f

docs.title: Small-cap funds see better score on liquidity stress-test. What does it mean?
docs.text:
Mint Money 
 Small-cap funds see better score on liquidity stress-test. What does it mean?
 Jash Kriplani 5 min read 22 Oct 2026, 11:41 AM IST 
 Summary
 Estimates show small-cap funds have shortened their portfolio liquidation time this year due to higher stock trading volumes, despite managing 30% more assets. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Small-cap mutual funds now need less time to sell their holdings in a stress scenario, even as the money they manage has grown by about 30% this year. As of September, the average small-cap fund would take 11.9 days to sell half its portfolio, down from 18.8 days in January. That is according to stress-test data that fund houses disclose for mid- and small-cap funds through the Association of Mutual Funds in India (Amfi). The time needed to sell a quarter of the portfolio has fallen to 6.2 days from 9.6 days. 
 These disclosures began in March 2024. Money had poured into small- and mid-cap funds through 2023, and valuations in the segment had risen sharply. Madhabi Puri Buch, who was chairperson of the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) at the time, had also flagged ‘pockets of froth’ in small- and mid-cap stocks. Fund houses began publishing stress-test results, first every fortnight and later every month. 
 When investors redeem, the fund must pay them within a few working days, and to raise that cash, it must sell stocks. Many small-cap stocks trade in small volumes, so selling a large holding quickly can push its price down. In a market fall, when many investors redeem at the same time, such forced selling pulls down the fund’s net asset value (NAV). The loss is borne by investors who stay on in the fund.
 The stress test shows how long this selling would take. The fewer the days, the easier it is for the fund to raise cash. The drop from 18.8 days to 11.9 days means the average small-cap fund is now better placed to handle a rush of redemptions, which lowers the risk of investments taking an extra hit in a sell-off. 
 Volume spike 
 Liquidity is a problem even when money comes in. In a thinly traded stock, a large buy order quickly consumes the shares on offer at the current price, so the fund ends up paying more for each subsequent lot. This is impact cost in reverse: the fund’s own buying pushes the price up. When heavy inflows need to be deployed quickly, they can artificially push up valuations. This is why several fund houses have, at different times, stopped or capped lump-sum investments in their small-cap funds, allowing only systematic investment plans ( SIPs ), often within limits.
 Small-cap fund assets rose to ₹ 4.61 trillion from ₹ 3.54 trillion between January and September. More money usually means bigger positions to sell, which should stretch liquidation time rather than shorten it. Valuations also rose, with the trailing 12-month price-to-earnings (PE) ratio of the Nifty Smallcap 250 index going up to 33x from 29x. Most of the fall in liquidation time came between January and June, when the average dropped to 11.4 days. It has stayed broadly at that level since. 
 Higher trading activity in small-cap stocks is a key reason. The average daily traded value of Nifty Smallcap 250 stocks on the National Stock Exchange ( NSE ) rose about 21% to ₹ 25,440 crore in April–September 2026, from ₹ 20,980 crore in the previous six months.
 This matters because the stress test is based on trading volumes. Under Amfi’s method, a fund excludes the least-liquid 20% of its portfolio and sells the remainder in proportion. It can sell no more than 10% of a stock’s daily trading volume, and the test assumes volume rises to three times normal levels. When stocks trade more, the same holding can be sold faster, so the estimated time falls. 
 What experts caution 
 “For small-cap funds with concentrated exposures, selling in bad markets can be tough when liquidity is thin. Large sell orders in thinly traded stocks push prices down further, adding to impact costs,” pointed out Deepak Jasani, an independent market expert. 
 “Investors should come into small-cap funds with a long time horizon so as to make the arithmetic of liquidation time irrelevant for their investments,” said Joydeep Sen, a corporate trainer (financial markets) and author. 
 Fund houses have to pay redemption proceeds within three working days, even in a falling market. What changes is the price investors get. The fund pays out at that day’s NAV, and if it has to sell stocks in a hurry to raise cash, those sales can pull the NAV down. 
 This is where the two risks of small-cap stocks come together. The first is volatility. Small-cap stocks tend to rise faster in good times and fall harder in bad times, which drives the high returns that attract many investors to these funds. The second is liquidity. Many of these stocks trade in small volumes, and in a sell-off, buyers step back just as sellers rush in. With few buyers around, large sell orders can push prices down further, adding to impact costs. Funds whose holdings are concentrated in fewer stocks can get hit harder. 
 The two risks can also feed each other. When the market falls, investors with a short horizon tend to redeem in panic. Funds then have to sell stocks to pay them, at a time when there are few buyers. That pushes prices and NAVs lower, which can trigger more redemptions. Those who exit in panic lock in their losses. Those who stay bear the cost of the forced selling. 
 Investors still need a long-term horizon 
 The stress test shows how exposed a fund is to such a cycle. A lower number is better, but it is only an estimate based on recent trading, and trading can dry up quickly in a fall. 
 Investors should use stress-test data as an indication of a fund’s ability to liquidate the portfolio in an extreme market scenario. When it comes to investing in small-cap funds, investors must remember that t

docs.title: Iran’s fleet of shadow tankers has run out of oil after monthslong US blockade
docs.text:
Global 
 Iran’s fleet of shadow tankers has run out of oil after monthslong US blockade
 Jon Emont , The Wall Street Journal 4 min read 22 Oct 2026, 06:57 AM IST 
 Summary
 Tehran had millions of barrels of crude in tankers floating in Asian waters that gave it a steady flow of much-needed cash. Now, that oil has dried up. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 For most of the war, Iran had an invaluable cushion: dozens of oil tankers holding millions of barrels of crude sitting safely in waters in Asia. Tehran steadily sold the oil to China, bringing in billions of much-needed cash.
 Now, that floating storage is gone. By mid-October, the reserves were fully depleted, according to analysts at Kpler, as a U.S. naval blockade prevented Iran from replacing the crude it normally sells to Chinese refineries.
 “There’s no more oil to discharge to China anymore,” said Homayoun Falakshahi, head of crude-oil analysis at Kpler.
 The drop in oil revenue is a further blow to Iran’s struggling economy, already facing runaway inflation and widespread shortages. U.S. Central Command, which is responsible for the Middle East, said Saturday that the blockade has denied Tehran at least $25 billion worth of oil revenue, which will, in turn, constrict Iran’s ability to replace destroyed factories and weapons.
 U.S. actions have “imposed devastating costs on Iran’s security apparatus,” said Adm. Brad Cooper, head of U.S. Central Command.
 Even as the U.S. pressure has choked off Iranian exports, oil from elsewhere in the Middle East is flowing, recently exceeding prewar levels, as U.S. protection helps secure the passage of non-Iranian oil through the Strait of Hormuz.
 The floating storage has been part of an elaborate system Iran developed over the years to get oil to its main customer, China, despite U.S. sanctions.
 Instead of sending oil directly to Chinese refineries, tankers linked to Iran ferried the crude to waters off the coast of Malaysia and Singapore. They then transferred the oil to other tankers that transported it to Chinese refineries. The subterfuge made it harder for the U.S. to track the flow of oil and punish sanctions violators. The waters off Malaysia and Singapore also became a useful place to store oil.
 Oil analysts say Chinese payments for Iranian oil can take around two months to arrive, meaning Tehran may still receive a trickle of funding from past sales in the weeks ahead.
 Iran has defied predictions that the blockade would collapse its economy and squeeze concessions on its nuclear program for more than six months. Tehran has stored oil in derelict tanks and trucked it to neighbors as the sea route shuts down.
 Still, the overall picture is grim for Iran’s economy. Falakshahi says oil sales represent around 30% to 40% of Iran’s government revenue and are its largest source of foreign exchange. A weakening Iranian currency, which has fallen by a third against the dollar since early July, is contributing to breakneck inflation.
 “It looks like the U.S. gamble is that the economy will either push the regime back into negotiations to accept a nuclear deal, or will spark protests internally which the regime will face challenges containing,” Falakshahi said.
 Alternative routes to export Iranian oil that don’t go through the Strait of Hormuz, like trucking oil overland, won’t come close to replacing the oil transported by sea, according to analysts.
 “Is it working? Yes, it’s working,” said Iman Nasseri, senior vice president of Middle East and Asia at energy-analytics company FGE NexantECA in Dubai, who once worked in the research arm of Iran’s oil ministry. Still, he said the regime has proven resilient in the past. “Let’s wait another year and see if the system can stand.”
 According to Kpler, by the start of the war in February, Iran had around 135 million barrels located overseas—much of it off the coast of Malaysia and Singapore—likely worth around $10 billion or more after the price of oil surged. When the U.S. first imposed a blockade on Iranian oil flows in April, Iran continued selling oil from this offshore reserve, with stores declining rapidly.
 When the U.S. lifted the blockade as part of peace negotiations in mid-June, Iran rushed out more oil, building back its reserves until the U.S. reimposed the blockade in mid-July. Those reserves, which had peaked at nearly 90 million barrels, fell to less than 1 million barrels by Oct. 5, and have since been completely exhausted, according to Kpler.
 Emma Li, an analyst at energy tracker Vortexa, also reported a major drop, estimating that there were about 6 million barrels of Iranian oil off Singapore as of Oct. 9. She said Chinese oil refineries are increasingly turning to alternative suppliers, including Brazil and West Africa.
 United Against Nuclear Iran, an advocacy group, also calculated that Iran’s oil exports had fallen to close to zero in August and September and that floating reserves in Southeast Asia had likely fallen to 10 million barrels or less by early October, saying the precise total was difficult to know. “They’ve got to be hurting,” said Charlie Brown, a UANI researcher. He said that while he couldn’t say that the reserves had gone to zero, “it seems likely to be well on the way to close to zero.”
 Iran’s government insists it can withstand the pressure. At a meeting of the International Monetary Fund in Bangkok last week, Abdolnaser Hemmati, governor of Iran’s central bank, said that despite pressure “the Iranian economy has demonstrated very good resilience, and the claim that Iran’s economy is collapsing is nothing more than an illusion.”
 Write to Jon Emont at jonathan.emont@wsj.com
