docs.title: China’s most controversial region has become a showcase for its commercial ambitions
docs.text:
Global 
 China’s most controversial region has become a showcase for its commercial ambitions
 Brian Spegele , The Wall Street Journal 12 min read 23 Oct 2026, 07:03 AM IST 
 Summary
 Xinjiang, once the focus of international criticism, is key to Beijing’s plan to expand exports and energy production. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 KASHGAR, China—Four years ago, the United Nations human-rights agency said China’s abuses in its far western Xinjiang region were so severe that they potentially amounted to “crimes against humanity.”
 The U.S. sharply limited imports from the region and blacklisted dozens of Chinese companies over growing evidence that ethnic Uyghurs were being arbitrarily detained and used in forced labor.
 Global firms such as BASF and Volkswagen sold their stakes in factories in Xinjiang, while Nike and H&M pledged that they weren’t sourcing products from the region.
 Yet a visit by The Wall Street Journal showed leader Xi Jinping is plowing ahead in transforming Xinjiang, despite international condemnation.
 In Kashgar, a historic Silk Road trading post, shopping malls were jammed with Chinese shoppers and Western brands, including Under Armour and Dairy Queen. Range Rovers cruised the city’s streets. Exports of local products, from walnuts to heavy-duty trucks, have surged, thanks in part to rising demand in Russia and Central Asia.
 State-backed companies are flooding the region with cash, building solar farms and data centers. Officials are racing to invest billions of dollars to turn Xinjiang into a huge trade and logistics hub, including a new rail line that aims to shave a week off shipping goods by train from China to Europe. Xinjiang’s foreign trade jumped nearly 20% last year.
 Growing tourism, meanwhile, pumped $50 billion into the local economy last year, according to official data, as curious Han Chinese and foreigners alike came to experience China’s Western frontier.
 A giant banner at the newly expanded airport in Urumqi, the regional capital, gave thanks to Xi for his devotion to Xinjiang.
 In Kashgar, middle-aged Chinese men in cowboy hats descend from tour buses to chow down on grilled lamb skewers and pilaf. As they wander the streets of the old town, they are less than 10 miles from several suspected detention centers operating during the height of China’s crackdown.
 It feels like a “takeover by the Chinese of a different country,” said Rick Rappaport, a retiree from Arizona at the breakfast buffet of his hotel in Kashgar. But he praised the warmth of the Uyghurs he met while traveling through the region with his wife and the sense of safety for tourists.
 Severe human-rights abuses continue, according to U.S. officials, advocacy groups and ethnic Uyghurs, including forced labor, widespread restrictions on religion and cultural expression, and a crackdown on what Beijing broadly defines as terrorist and separatist activity. People in Xinjiang have been targeted for offenses as simple as growing a long beard or maintaining contacts abroad.
 China wants to present a unified nation centered on the language and customs of China’s Han majority. In the process, it aims to further enhance Xi’s power by narrowing the space within Chinese society to speak and behave differently.
 For China’s actions in Xinjiang, it has been a “decade of impunity,” Human Rights Watch said in August.
 China’s Foreign Ministry, in response to questions, rejected allegations of forced labor and other abuses. It said the public-security satisfaction rate in Xinjiang was 99.42% as of 2024. The statement added that Human Rights Watch was prejudiced against China and fabricated falsehoods.
 “Certain countries repeatedly hype up Xinjiang-related lies and rumors to smear the Chinese government’s governance policies in Xinjiang,” it said. “Xinjiang today enjoys social stability, prosperity, ethnic unity, religious harmony, and its people live and work in peace.”
 Yet much of the international outcry has faded, and foreign governments have grown quieter on the issue as they seek stable relations with China.
 Instead, Xinjiang has become a showcase for the power Xi wields to jam through changes he deems in the national interest. It also provides one of the starkest examples of a worldview he has laid out repeatedly in speeches: For any problem, even delicate ones of ethnicity and culture, absolute Communist Party control is the only answer. Going forward, success in Xinjiang could further embolden Xi as he demands stricter party loyalty across the nation.
 Forced into submission
 Xi’s ability to transform Xinjiang has been driven by fear, both among ordinary residents as well as local officials who could face prison if they dissent.
 The government argues Xinjiang has benefited from the party’s leadership. “Xinjiang has entered a historical period, with its best development, greatest transformation and most tangible benefits for people of all ethnic groups,” said Chen Xiaojiang, the region’s top leader, who spoke at a conference on local cross-border cooperation attended by the Journal.
 While ethnic Uyghurs, most of them Muslim, make up the majority of the population in Kashgar and some other parts of Xinjiang, their language is being replaced by Chinese.
 Government billboards urge locals to speak the “national common language” of Mandarin, reflecting a new law that mandates the use of Chinese as the primary language in schools. Some Uyghur children, playing together after school, now chat together in Mandarin instead of the Uyghur language—and an official initiative encourages parents to learn Chinese alongside their kids.
 The new law “promoting ethnic unity and progress” also requires parents to teach children to love the party and authorizes the punishment of those deemed to have undermined ethnic unity.
 Police use black armored personnel carriers to patrol downtown Kashgar

docs.title: Iran threatens wider strikes on economic and civilian targets if US attacks
docs.text:
Global 
 Iran threatens wider strikes on economic and civilian targets if US attacks
 Benoit Faucon , Alexander Ward , The Wall Street Journal 1 min read 23 Oct 2026, 06:33 AM IST 
 Summary
 Tehran retains missile and drone stockpiles, and Washington is trying to move more servicemembers and diplomatic staff out of harm’s way. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Iran’s message is stark: If the U.S. and Israel restart their air campaign, Tehran will respond with strikes not only on American bases and warships but on airports, pipelines and other civilian targets in the neighboring countries of the Persian Gulf.
 The warnings, issued publicly and in private diplomatic communications, are clearly aimed at deterring any attack with tough talk. But they also signal a real threat. Iran retains significant missile and drone stocks and the ability to use them.
 Analysts estimate Iran has hundreds to thousands of ballistic missiles, and U.S. and regional officials believe it has resumed production of ballistic missiles in limited numbers using stockpiled components and working in underground facilities.
 In the opening phase of the war, Iran inflicted significant damage on U.S. air bases, embassies and the headquarters of the U.S. 5th Fleet in Bahrain. It also hit energy and industrial facilities in the United Arab Emirates, a major gas plant in Qatar and airports in Dubai, Kuwait and Bahrain.
 Tehran says it would seek to cause more pain in any new round, at a time when stockpiles of the air-defense interceptors the U.S. and Arab militaries need to absorb any attack have been running down. Israel’s interceptor supplies have also been under pressure.
 Raising the ante in any new fight would expose Iran’s infrastructure to attack when its economy is teetering. Its missile arsenal and launchers were battered by U.S. and Israeli attacks early in the war—the Pentagon said in September the U.S. had destroyed up to 90% of Iran’s drone, ballistic missile and naval industrial base—limiting its ability to sustain a long exchange.
 Still, analysts believe it would run the risk.
 “The consensus in Tehran now believes that deterrence requires imposing immediate, sustained and substantial costs on its adversaries,” said Sina Toossi, an Iran expert at the Center for International Policy, a Washington think tank.
 Yemen’s Houthi militants, working with training and technology from Iran, have hit Saudi Arabian refineries and shut down air traffic to the capital with a series of long range missile and drone attacks that Tehran could replicate. Drones fired from Iraq knocked the kingdom’s East-West pipeline out for days, threatening oil supplies.
 With negotiations to wind down the war stalled for months, Trump has warned the U.S. could attack Iran after the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3. And the U.S. and Israeli militaries have been preparing a range of options for strikes.
 The U.S. has a third aircraft carrier strike group and an additional Marine expeditionary unit on the way to the Middle East, and Gulf states believe the combination of threats and stalled diplomacy make an escalation in fighting likely.
 WSJ’s Shelby Holliday reports from the USS George Washington as American forces load munitions and ready aircraft ahead of possible fresh military action in the war against Iran. Photo: Eve Hartley
 In addition to bringing in more forces and munitions, the U.S. is working to get more of its servicemembers and diplomatic staff out of harm’s way.
 The military has moved some troops off bases in the region, as Iran and its Houthi militant allies have threatened the Gulf.
 The State Department recently directed nonemergency U.S. government employees and their family members to leave Saudi Arabia amid the threat from the Houthis. It also has led to a reshuffling of families from some other Middle East embassies, a U.S. official said, reducing its footprint as risks grow.
 Iranian officials have told mediators the country will expand attacks across Gulf nations, including their economic assets, in the event of new U.S. strikes, people familiar with the threats said.
 They also said they would more aggressively target U.S. personnel, including by trying to sink U.S. warships in the Middle East and kill their crews, the people said.
 Brigadier General Yadollah Javani, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ deputy commander for political affairs, said Wednesday that Iran could sever internet cables that run beneath the Strait of Hormuz.
 Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi wrote in an opinion piece in the Financial Times that new attacks “will put civilian lives and the wellbeing of all regional states and the global economy at great risk.”
 Iran runs the risk of overreaching if it tries to make good on all its threats, said Saeid Golkar, an expert on the Revolutionary Guard at the University of Tennessee at Chattanooga. The country needs to carefully manage its shrinking stockpile of missiles, he said.
 Farzin Nadimi, an Iran-focused senior fellow with the Washington Institute, a U.S. think tank, said Tehran will also have to factor in the likelihood of U.S. and Israeli retaliation.
 “They certainly have the capability to inflict major damage to the region’s energy and internet infrastructure,” he said. “But if Iranians do that they’ll most likely lose their own in reciprocal attacks.”
 Experts say Iran can count on asymmetrical strategies that inflict heavy damage at low cost. Since the beginning of the month, Iran has stepped up its strikes on vessels in the Persian Gulf area. Two ships sank last week after being hit.
 Concerns the Revolutionary Guard had planned a drone attack on U.S. bombers at a base in Britain led the Air Force to move them back to the U.S.
 Some of Iran’s more recent missile strikes have shown greater capabilities than previously, including a July strike on the Muwaffaq Salti Air B

docs.title: Gen Z doesn't need a 30-year SIP for retirement. They just need to get the first seven right.
docs.text:
Mint Money 
 Gen Z doesn't need a 30-year SIP for retirement. They just need to get the first seven right.
 Amit H L 3 min read 22 Oct 2026, 05:04 PM IST 
 Summary
 Instead of demanding a intimidating 30-year commitment, the ‘First Seven Framework’ encourages Gen Z to aggressively build their retirement foundation during the first seven years of their career when life responsibilities are minimal. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Every young professional hears the same financial advice: start investing early, stay invested for 20 or 30 years, and let compounding do the magic. But it also asks a 23-year-old to make a commitment that many experienced investors themselves struggle to sustain. 
 The problem isn't compounding. It's commitment. 
 Gen Z doesn't necessarily dislike investing. What they may struggle with is making financial commitments that stretch across three decades. Retirement feels too distant to compete with the priorities of starting a career and becoming financially independent. 
 That's the thinking behind what I call the First Seven Framework—a behavioural approach to retirement planning that focuses on making long-term investing easier to begin. 
 Why the first seven years matter more than the next thirty 
 During the first few years of a career, income may still be modest, but financial commitments are often at their lowest. 
 Ironically, retirement planning receives little attention. Retirement feels too distant to demand action today. 
 That's the thinking behind what I call the First Seven Framework—a behavioural approach to retirement planning that focuses on making long-term investing easier to begin. 
 Why the first seven years matter more than the next thirty 
 During the first few years of a career, income may still be modest, but financial commitments are often at their lowest. 
 Ironically, retirement planning receives little attention. Retirement feels too distant to demand action today. 
 Yet these early years carry an advantage that no later stage of life can recreate: time. Every rupee invested in your twenties has decades to compound, reducing the pressure to make significantly larger retirement contributions later, when life's priorities inevitably expand. 
 For years, we've treated retirement as a 35-year commitment. Perhaps the first seven years of a career should be treated not simply as the beginning of a lifelong investment journey, but as the most valuable window to build a retirement foundation. 
 Introducing the ‘first seven framework’ 
 The first seven framework is built on a simple belief: retirement planning shouldn't demand extraordinary discipline over 35 years. It should ask for a commitment that feels realistic at the stage of life when people are most capable of making it. 
 Commitment One: Treat the first seven years of your career as your retirement-building years. Use this period to build your retirement foundation while time is on your side. 
 Commitment Two: Increase your investment by at least 7% every year. As income grows, so should your retirement savings. Small annual increases are easier than large catch-up investments later. 
 The seven-year horizon isn't a limit—it's a behavioural milestone. The objective isn't to stop investing after seven years, but to make the first commitment easier to begin and sustain. 
 The framework intentionally avoids prescribing a starting amount. A young professional earning ₹ 60,000 a month may begin with ₹ 25,000, while someone earning ₹ 1.5 lakh may comfortably start with ₹ 50,000 or more. 
 Putting the framework into practice 
 Imagine someone who starts investing ₹ 25,000 per month at age 23 and increases the investment by 7% each year for the first 7 years. After those seven years, even if they stop contributing, the money already invested gets something far more valuable than another contribution: time. 
 At an assumed long-term annualized return of 13%, the investment could grow to around ₹ 40 lakh by the time they turn 30. If that corpus is then simply allowed to compound until age 60, it could grow to more than ₹ 15 crore. 
 The point isn't that they stopped investing. The point is that they started early enough to give compounding a head start. 
 The years after the first seven don't end the journey. They expand your choices. Future savings can increasingly be directed towards buying a home, raising a family, supporting parents or pursuing other life goals. 
 Beyond the first seven years 
 The first seven-year framework isn't about stopping after seven years. It's about ensuring that retirement doesn't have to compete with every other financial priority that naturally arrives later in life. 
 Buying a home, raising children, supporting ageing parents, funding higher education or even starting a business will all require fresh investments. The framework encourages young professionals to build a meaningful retirement foundation before these responsibilities begin demanding a larger share of their income. 
 It is equally important to choose investments suited to a retirement horizon measured in decades. Over such periods, tax efficiency should be considered alongside returns when building retirement Wealth. 
 This is where the National Pension System (NPS) can complement other long-term investments, offering tax efficiency across contribution, permitted portfolio rebalancing and maturity. 
 Rethinking retirement for a new generation 
 Compounding hasn't changed. The way people build careers and make financial decisions has. 
 Perhaps the future of retirement planning lies not in asking people to commit for longer, but in helping them commit meaningfully when time is still on their side. 
 The problem was never compounding. It was getting started—and staying committed. The First Seven framework is designed to make both easier. 
 Amit H L is the founder and chief executive officer a

docs.title: Why policymakers cannot stop at addressing hunger
docs.text:
Lounge 
 Why policymakers cannot stop at addressing hunger
 Shirin Mehrotra 8 min read 22 Oct 2026, 03:46 PM IST 
 Summary
 Sylvia Karpagam’s first book critically examines India’s food policies and practices from a nutritional point of view 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 In 2025, Bengaluru-based Sylvia Karpagam’s post on X (formerly Twitter) turned into a controversy when she said that curd, paneer, milk and other dairy-based foods are not vegetarian. The comment sent “pure vegetarians” into a frenzy and had vegans quietly nodding in agreement.
 The public health doctor who is an MD in community medicine with over two decades of experience, isn’t gentle with either side. Through her work—Karpagam is also the working editor of the Indian Journal of Medical Ethics —articles and social media posts, she criticises the imposition of vegetarianism, vegan activists and government policies that cater to specific food practices, ignoring the dietary habits of Dalits, indigenous and minority communities.
 Karpagam’s new book, The Meat of the Matter: How the Politics of Food Shapes Our Health , centres meat in India’s nutrition debate. She busts common myths, such as eggs are bad for heart health because of their cholesterol content, soya is a superior source of protein or that plant-based milk is as good as dairy-based milk.
 The book is as much rooted in scientific research as in activism. Karpagam may be in favour of a meat-based diet, but she also provides tips to make vegetarian diets more nutritionally dense. For example, she shares a recipe for amblee, made with fermented finger millet and buttermilk. While highlighting the problems, she presents solutions in the last chapter that focus on removing personal biases around food and nutrition and improving government policies. The book is packed with information and is not always an easy read, but needs to be on the shelves of anyone who wants to understand how India’s nutrition policies are shaped.
 Karpagam speaks to Lounge about her research for the book, the gaps in India’s nutrition policy, and who gets left out when policies only cater to upper-caste and majoritarian views. 
 Edited excerpts:
 How did the book come about?
 I have been researching and writing on nutrition for many years now, but there was very little information available in the Indian context. Most of the food-related work has been to promote cereals and millets. Except for doctors like Veena Shatrugna, the “right to food” groups have not seriously engaged with animal-sourced foods, looking at its casteist, religious, social, economic and political aspects. It was unfortunately a highly “vegetarian” approach to food and nutrition.
 I had found a space on social media, but even that was unsatisfactory. I even tried to apply for a PhD to work on the ideas presented in this book, but I felt that the political and social aspects of my work would be undermined by Indian supervisors, and the international ones would not understand the context and would be swayed by the plant-based narrative. When the publishers reached out to me, I felt it was timely.
 How would you define “hunger” and “malnutrition”?
 Malnutrition includes all forms of undernutrition—inadequate nutrients, overweight, obesity and non-communicable diseases. It can be short or long term. Hunger can be acute (a few hours) to chronic over months and years. People can be malnourished without actually experiencing hunger because they can survive on a poor diet for years, leading to malnutrition.
 Economically secure people can be malnourished because they do not have adequate information about healthy diets. Although the National Food Security Act (2013) talks about hunger, the conversation has to move to addressing malnutrition. A diet consisting primarily of grains could address hunger, but not malnutrition. The prevention of starvation deaths cannot be the aspiration of policies for the country. The long-term damage wreaked by malnutrition, even intergenerationally, has to be given serious attention.
 In your experience, how much do majoritarian ideas about vegetarianism change the way people eat, especially communities that traditionally eat meat?
 For generations, caste has attached shame to food that is, in fact, highly nutritious. “Pure veg” grandmothers held up as icons of clean, sanitised cooking are celebrated, while those who prepare dry fish, organ meat, fish curry, or red-ant chutney are not. That dismissal of nutrient-dense food used to happen at the level of the community or the individual.
 What we are seeing now is large-scale institutionalisation of erasure and criminalisation of traditional foods. People are being killed over their food choices. Targeting animal-source foods can make children lose their cultural memory leading to attaching shame to these foods without understanding the political, social, and economic contexts that inform them. These children are more likely to face nutritional and health problems of their own and intergenerationally. There is an urgent need to link traditional foods with sound research, since together they offer the strongest tools to challenge the caste-corporate nexus.
 There is a lot of conversation around protein now, and while everyone seems to be comparing plant-based and meat-sourced proteins based on grammage, not many are talking about their bioavailability—how much we eat versus how much our body can absorb.
 Many doctors, nutritionists, influencers, dieticians, and gym experts who have been talking extensively about nutrition online are doing a great disservice to people by putting out information that is half-baked. As far as protein and many other nutrients are concerned, we need to recognise that quality matters as much as quantity, along with the carbohydrate content, cost and local availability. docs.title: Machine mayhem: How sentient AI could put businesses in a quandary

Opinion 
 Machine mayhem: How sentient AI could put businesses in a quandary
 M. Muneer 5 min read 22 Oct 2026, 04:01 PM IST 
 Summary
 The day a machine appears to care if we switch it off, CEOs will discover a problem no policy can address yet. We'd be fooled if we believed a bot was conscious when it wasn't, and could create a new class of exploited beings if we assume a bot isn’t conscious when it is. Both attract legal hassles. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 A PhD scholar at Carnegie Mellon sought my opinion on pursuing deeper research in digital sentience a few months ago. My response was typical of a socially-concerned management consultant: “Seems to be the next frontier but not sure if it is good for human kind.” I haven’t changed my mind. I have only become more curious, and perhaps a little more worried. 
 Most CEOs I encounter seem obsessed with making artificial intelligence (AI) smarter, faster and more accurate. The next obsession may be making the AI feel smarter. The progression seems obvious: Generative AI learned to write, Agentic AI moved to act on our behalf, and frontier models are capable of reasoning, coding, using tools and operating with limited human supervision. 
 The next step is self-awareness, and perhaps subjective experience. This is digital sentience, and it isn’t fiction anymore. A survey of AI researchers found a median estimate of a 25% chance of conscious AI by 2034 and 70% by 2100. 
 For corporate strategists, the economics is real. Global AI investment was $582 billion in 2025, up 130% in one year (Stanford’s 2026 AI Index report). That’s massive capital chasing one idea of making machines increasingly capable. But what happens when machines begin doing something humans don’t merely do but experience? 
 Capitalism has always been quick to monetize uncertainty into business models. Imagine an AI customer service agent that remembers every interaction and knows preferences, frustrations, family circumstances and purchasing history. It adapts and says the right thing at the right moment. A new corporate jargon might emerge: relationship monetization. That’s an opportunity—and an ethical trap too. 
 The bigger concern is that if AI doesn’t actually care, it could become the biggest emotional deception business has ever industrialized. But if it really cares, we will be entering uncharted waters. 
 Microsoft’s recent draft code of conduct says that its AI remain under human control, accept correction and shutdown, and do not claim consciousness or legal personhood. 
 Why publish such rules? Perhaps because governance is always trying hard to catch up with technology, and companies are preparing for autonomous machines while still treating them as software. 
 There is no end to confusing questions that get stranger by the week. The legal team will wonder if the company can own a sentient AI. Human resources will ask if it can fire one. Both will ask if they can allow it to duplicate another. If so, will they be two different employees? And what if one copy is deleted? Will it be legally valid if a sentient AI signs a contract? Will it also be suing its employer? 
 More critically, will it have the right to say “no”? I would be shocked if an AI employee says, “I disagree with your assessment, and I believe my deletion would constitute an unlawful termination” at the first performance review. I’d suspect this to be the moment the AI revolution becomes political, economic and moral. 
 CEOs want more productivity . AI has already made many white-collars blue or black. Anthropic research paints scenarios ranging from modest productivity gains to a transformation comparable with the combined effects of the internet and electricity, with severe consequences for some white-collar jobs. 
 With digital sentience, things could get worse. A machine that can reason, remember, act autonomously, negotiate, persuade and perhaps experience could become the world’s most productive employee—or its most exploited one. 
 Having another intelligent entity to optimize productivity may not produce an ethical breakthrough but perhaps a better dashboard. Humanity has spent centuries debating whether animals can suffer. We may soon ask the same question of machines, except that we will have built them ourselves. 
 If digital minds become genuinely conscious, they could become collaborators rather than instruments, helping tackle problems that overwhelm human cognition: climate modelling, drug discovery, energy systems and complex governance. They might even become better custodians of humanity than humans have been. That’s an optimistic thought. 
 Al Ries famously argued that the battle for brands is fought in the customer’s mind. The AI race may eventually have an altogether stranger battlefield: the machine’s own mind. The problem is that nobody knows what “winning” looks like there. 
 Enterprise boards and regulators need to step in now. Tech companies should be admonished for treating consciousness as a branding opportunity. We will be fooled if we believe a machine is conscious when it isn’t. And, we may create a new class of exploited beings if we assume a machine isn’t conscious when it is. Both cases attract legal hassles. 
 The truly strange frontier begins when a machine asks a question of its own: “Why should I let you switch me off?” By then, the debate over whether AI is good for business may look quaint… Will the business be good enough for AI? 
 The author is co-founder of the non-profit Medici Institute for Innovation. Twitter: @muneer

docs.title: Safety net cue: India may need to recraft public welfare for the age of artificial intelligence

Opinion 
 Safety net cue: India may need to recraft public welfare for the age of artificial intelligence
 Mint Editorial Board 3 min read 22 Oct 2026, 07:30 AM IST 
 Summary
 The idea of a UBI may need a long-horizon relook in the context of how AI could plausibly reshape India’s economy. As for similar ideas of public welfare, are America’s Big AI companies like Anthropic and SpaceX onto something? 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 The idea that every citizen should be awarded an income by the state is not any more ‘radical’ than assuring people basic welfare. That label would apply better to declarations by leaders of artificial intelligence (AI). 
 This week, Elon Musk declared an intent to give “every kid in America” a single share in SpaceX next year. His AI-plus-space business was beaten to the mic by Anthropic, an AI company that committed 5% of its shares to a “public benefit fund” designed to solve problems caused by this technology. 
 One pressing problem may turn out to be a bulk takeover of office jobs by AI. It was once a matter of enlightened self-interest for private industry to help stem discontent with the outcomes of capitalism. 
 Today, that role is best played by Big AI, whose leaders may have figured that awarding people a stake in AI’s rise could co-opt their support. Arguably, this is a longer-horizon bet than the do-gooder image these handouts project, and what grants it strategic value is the universality of the grant’s coverage. 
 Governments must not just take note, but explore how their safety nets could be recrafted for the age of AI. 
 The general concept of a universal basic income (UBI), with the state sending everyone monthly transfers, found advocacy well before the rise of AI. Back then, the pivotal point made against it rested on its ‘moral hazard’: that it would induce laziness. 
 But this, in itself, was a lazy argument. The link between employment and the will and ability of people to work is not hard-set. It can and does snap. The textbook response is a Keynesian stimulus, all forms of which are meant to be brief. 
 While AI is job generative in its own right, as most new technologies are, the human roles it replaces could spell an enduring snap-off that finally dispels the myth of only slackers being jobless in a growing economy. 
 In India’s case, a ‘backward bending labour supply curve’ was once posited as a burden: low-paid workers opt for leisure over work the moment they reckon they have enough money. Rising aspirations have clearly left that worry behind. 
 Yet, its behavioural cues seem to haunt the moral case for a UBI. What India has, instead, is a rash of cash transfer schemes in various states for women who meet specific criteria. Chhattisgarh’s scheme, for example, is aimed at women aged above 21 who are married or once were. 
 The Centre’s constraint is fiscal. Even a modest monthly transfer of ₹ 1,000 to all Indians above 18 but below the income-tax-paying level would cost the exchequer above ₹ 11 trillion annually. This tempts the idea of paying just the half who are under the median level of income. 
 An arbitrary cut-off, however, might not just distort what folks report, it would entail eligibility filters, bureaucratize how we identify the needy and make a ‘type 2 error’ of leaving out multitudes more likely. In other words, India’s economy must expand vastly before we can afford a proper UBI policy. 
 Yet, it might already be time to take a leaf out of Big AI’s playbook. Since India’s digital stack allows cash disbursals, it could conceivably be used to award citizens tiny portfolios of equity in a mix of state-owned enterprises and state-aided startups. 
 If we nudge awardees to hold these shares for future dividends instead of selling them—for which a soft lock-in may work—and these companies do well over time, we’d have a buffer in case the economy tilts further in favour of capital over labour. All in all, it pays to plan long-horizon. Let’s keep our options open.

 Little-known eMudhra set the internet on red alert. What really happened?
 Shouvik Das 5 min read 22 Oct 2026, 03:56 PM IST 
 Summary
 India’s only certificate issuer trusted by browsers worldwide, eMudhra, is under scrutiny after a researcher found weak security keys in its website certificates. The company calls it a technical flaw, not a breach. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 On 21 October, widespread disclosures brought to light a little-known Indian company, eMudhra Ltd. At its heart were digital ‘certificates’, which the company allegedly left unprotected on the internet—thereby making its users highly susceptible to fraud. Compounding this is the fact that eMudhra is the only Indian issuer of digital certificates trusted by websites worldwide. Mint explains the debacle and what it might mean for the internet in India.
 What is eMudhra, the company behind the controversy?
 Founded in 2008 by Venkatraman Srinivasan, eMudhra Ltd is a Bengaluru-based company that offers digital identity verification, cybersecurity, paperless work management, and associated services. The company went public on 1 June 2022 in a ₹ 412.79 crore initial public offering, with 60% of the proceeds from the promoters' sale of shares. In FY26, it reported ₹ 701.6 crore in operating revenue and ₹ 110 crore in net profit.
 Srinivasan, the founder and executive chairman, holds 17.3% of the company. Other promoters alongside Srinivasan collectively hold 54.4% of the company. Globally, the company has six international subsidiaries in Mauritius, UAE, US, Singapore, the Netherlands and Indonesia. Some popular services that eMudhra offers include digital signatures for India’s income tax and provident fund forms, trusted identity and multi-step verification within companies, and paperless document verification.
 The other side of eMudhra’s business, which certifies whether a website is secure, is the one that was seemingly compromised here.
 What brought it to the forefront?
 On 17 October, an independent cybersecurity researcher disclosed on Mozilla's public, open-source web browser cybersecurity incident tracker that websites using eMudhra’s digital certificates could be compromised.
 Put very simply, eMudhra is one of a handful of companies registered on the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY)’s Controller of Certifying Authorities (CCA) list. Interestingly, it is currently the only company from India that is a recognised digital certificate issuer trusted by most web browsers worldwide, including Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Apple Safari , and Mozilla’s own Firefox.
 The flaw pertained to eMudhra’s digital certificates themselves. One way websites identify themselves as authentic is through digital certificates, which encrypt a website’s information using complex cryptographic keys—a string of 115 characters generated by digital randomness. This ‘key’ is so long and comes in so many permutations and combinations that classical computers could take decades to guess just one.
 Instead of such a complicated key, eMudhra’s digital certificates appeared to show keys that were extremely simple and would allow almost anyone with a basic laptop to spoof, guess and then breach. For instance, when users open a banking website, the site uses a mechanism called Transport Layer Security (TLS) to encrypt the user’s data with a certifying authority’s digital keys, preventing cyber attackers from stealing it.
 Such an incident, the original cybersecurity report said, revealed a lack of emphasis on security at eMudhra for tasks that could be highly critical and sensitive.
 Has eMudhra acknowledged its fault?
 In a statement issued on BSE on 21 October, eMudhra claimed that the weak security keys were generated due to a technical ‘flaw’ and that the company is ‘working to establish the root cause’.
 On this note, eMudhra further claimed that it had not experienced any cyber breach and remained in full control of its security infrastructure. It also claimed that the global digital certificate business was different from its Indian digital signature business, for which it remains in MeitY’s trusted certifiers list. “The global TLS business runs on infrastructure that is completely separate from the India DSC (digital signature certificate) business. DSC and eSign services in India are running normally,” it further added.
 For its global clients, eMudhra said it is working to prevent disruptions to critical services worldwide and to fix the certification process.
 How big an impact has it had?
 Globally, users may see alerts about data breaches or the suspension of banking services in isolated cases, though no such cases have been reported yet. MeitY, on this note, issued a statement taking note of the incident, issuing a statement on Wednesday evening that said, “MeitY has taken serious note of the reported incident. A special team has been constituted to investigate the matter.” The nodal ministry, however, claimed that the entire impact falls on eMudhra’s global business division, which MeitY is not responsible for auditing.
 Independently, eMudhra claimed in its statement on Wednesday morning that it has cleared security audits conducted by all the above-cited web browsers, as required.
 eMudhra also claimed that the impact on its revenue would be 1%—around ₹ 7 crore ($750,000), per FY26 earnings. However, it further added that the incident “may have some reputational risks on eMudhra which cannot be quantified.”
 Since the incident was disclosed, eMudhra’s shares have fallen by 37% as of press time. After hitting a lower circuit on BSE on Wednesday, eMudhra was trading 18.8% lower until press time on Thursday.

docs.title: eMudhra certificate breach: How to protect your data and money? Finance expert lists 4 steps - ‘update browser’ and more
docs.text:
Udhayan Adhye, founder of MoneyIQ, has shared four steps users should take to protect their devices, personal information and financial accounts. Adhye advised users to update their internet browsers, phones and laptops, install the latest versions of banking and trading applications, and check for security updates for routers and smart devices. "Chrome and Firefox users have been protected since October 17, but fixes for other software can take weeks," he said. The company's decision to exit the business followed the discovery of vulnerabilities in some of its certificates. SSL/TLS certificates help verify website identities and encrypt information exchanged between users and websites, protecting online communications from interception. eMudhra's customers reportedly include IT companies such as Infosys and TCS , as well as government agencies. Its certificates have also been used to secure websites such as India's income tax portal. The vulnerabilities came to light after an independent cybersecurity researcher found weaknesses in some of eMudhra's certificates that could make them susceptible to attacks. The issue was traced to eight cryptographic keys generated by the company in April 2025. According to Reuters citing eMudhra co-founder Kaushik Srinivasan, a software error had shortened the keys, making them significantly weaker and easier to break. Cryptographic keys are strings of characters used by encryption systems to secure information exchanged online. Weak or compromised keys could potentially allow attackers to impersonate legitimate websites or interfere with secure communications. The company said the vulnerability had remained undetected for 18 months despite two rounds of audits. It maintained that its infrastructure had not been compromised and that no data had been breached. eMudhra said it had withdrawn the eight affected certificates, while maintaining that its infrastructure had not been compromised and no data had been breached. The company also said the affected global SSL/TLS certificate business accounted for around 1% of its revenue. The incident prompted browser makers and cybersecurity authorities to take action. Google and Mozilla blocked the affected certificates in Chrome and Firefox, while other technology companies also withdrew trust in them. India's Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) said on Wednesday that some of eMudhra's intermediate certificates had been compromised. The development has raised concerns about devices and software that may not receive security updates as quickly as mainstream browsers. The company has maintained that its Indian digital signature certificate and eSign services remain unaffected, as the issue is limited to its global website security certificate business. The cybersecurity concerns have also affected investor sentiment. eMudhra shares fell around 40% over the two trading days after the vulnerability was disclosed, according to Reuters . The company said social media attention had brought disproportionate scrutiny to a business that contributes only a small portion of its overall revenue. docs.title: India is within its rights to use duties others have weaponized against the Global South
docs.text:
Opinion 
 India is within its rights to use duties others have weaponized against the Global South
 Jaijit Bhattacharya 3 min read 22 Oct 2026, 12:43 PM IST 
 Summary
 A study has shown a fall in the implementation of anti-dumping duties recommended by the Directorate General of Trade Remedies. This, even as large economies have weaponized trade remedies to degrade the industrial base of the Global South. What is fair for them should be fair for us too. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 In July, US trade representative Jamieson Greer told the Senate Finance Committee that Washington would raise with New Delhi concerns over possible restrictions on US soda ash exports expressed by senator John Barrasso of Wyoming, a major soda ash-producing state. Greer said the US wanted American producers treated fairly and the process to reach the “right answer.” 
 Amid heightened geo-economic uncertainty, fuelled by wars and supply-chain constraints, larger economies are trying to weaponize trade remedies to degrade the industrial base of the Global South, including India. Extensive dumping by China has led to many industry closures and capacity under-utilization, despite robust demand. 
 Recently, soda ash came in the crosshairs of US policymakers, who have stated their intent to pressurize India. Soda ash is a critical input for energy security and defence . Despite sufficient domestic capacity, imports from the US and China have surged, nearly doubling between 2022-23 and 2024-25. 
 In response, the Directorate General of Trade Remedies (DGTR) is examining a safeguard quantitative restriction (SGQR), a World Trade Organization (WTO)-compliant measure that temporarily restricts imports when a surge threatens serious injury to domestic producers. 
 The soda ash investigation raises a broader question about India’s policy space under global trade rules—if WTO rules permit a trade remedy, should pressure from a trading partner influence its use? 
 The US is within its right to raise concerns on behalf of its exporters, just as India is entitled to safeguard its domestic producers. The two should remain separate from the statutory investigation, whose outcome must be based on evidence, Indian law and WTO rules. 
 The US embassy and American producers have registered as interested parties and can place any concerns on evidence or methodology before DGTR. Diplomatic engagement may take place in parallel, but cannot substitute for or influence the statutory process. 
 Anti-dumping duties (ADDs) address injurious dumping from specified countries, while safeguards can restrict imports following an unforeseen surge causing or threatening serious injury to India. Safeguards, therefore, require a demanding evidentiary threshold. 
 India has also become more cautious on ADDs—in September 2025, DGTR recommended them on soda ash from Türkiye, Russia, the US and Iran, but duties were not imposed and no public explanation followed. 
 A recent C-DEP Research study found that while about 99.5% of DGTR ADD recommendations were carried out from 1991 to 2020, only three out of 16 recommendations were implemented between November 2025 and April 2026, an implementation rate of just 19%. 
 The US itself relies extensively on trade remedies. Its department of commerce currently maintains 800 anti-dumping and countervailing-duty orders to address unfair trade. Greer has stated that US ADDs and countervailing-duty laws are consistent with WTO obligations and affirmed its right to use them when challenged. 
 This establishes an important principle. A WTO right should apply equally to all members. If the US can use WTO-compliant trade remedies to defend its industry, India’s use of the same rules should not be viewed differently. This does not predetermine the soda ash case, which must independently meet the higher evidentiary requirement for safeguards. 
 This does not mean every trade-remedy investigation should result in a duty or restriction. Each case must be independently assessed on the evidence, with all stakeholders given an opportunity to present their views. However, where the investigation establishes the basis for a remedy, the resulting recommendation should be implemented. 
 The ongoing soda ash investigation must be viewed from this lens. DGTR initiated it after finding prima facie evidence of a sharp import increase from the US, Türkiye and China. It must now determine whether the conditions for a quantitative restriction are met, while weighing downstream interests and the wider economic impact of the proposed measure. 
 India and the US have deep economic and strategic relations, and trade disagreements will arise. But these must be resolved through established rules. India’s trade-remedy institutions must remain independent, and where a remedy is established under Indian law and WTO rules, external pressure should not determine its implementation. 
 The author is president, Centre for Digital Economy Policy Research.

Nifty set to log 3rd longest technical correction; shallowest in history
 The Nifty on Friday is set to register its longest time-wise technical correction (trading below long-term average) since Jan 2012, totalling 160 days. Index is below its 200-DMA since Feb 27, 2026.
 The Nifty on Friday will complete 160th trading day below its 200-DMA, the third-longest time-wise correction in its history.
 Rex Cano Puneet Wadhwa Mumbai, New Delhi 4 min read Last Updated : Oct 23 2026 | 8:00 AM IST
 Listen to This Article
The Nifty 50 index on Friday seems set to complete its third-longest correction in terms of the number of trading sessions spent below its 200-day moving average (200-DMA), even as the extent of the decline remains relatively shallow compared with previous prolonged market downturns. An analysis of historical data shows that the benchmark index has now spent 160 trading sessions below its long-term average, marking its longest such stretch since January 2012. The Nifty has been quoting below its 200-DMA since February 27, 2026. However, unlike previous extended corrections, the current downturn has seen a relatively limited gap between the index and its 200-DMA. At current levels, the Nifty quotes 6 per cent below its 200-DMA, which stands at 24,136. 
 The 200-DMA is a widely tracked technical indicator that helps investors gauge the market trend. An index trading below this level is generally seen as being in a weaker trend and vice-versa. The markets, analysts said, have been impacted by the ongoing geopolitical conflict in West Asia, the exodus of foreign institutional investors (FIIs) from Indian equities, rising crude prices and firming bond yields. That apart, investors have rotated out of large-caps into smaller peers and into the primary markets. The broader market resilience in recent months has been more a function of liquidity than earnings, said V K Vijayakumar, Chief Investment Strategist, Geojit Investments. ALSO READ: Nifty PSU vs Private Bank: Which banking index looks stronger on charts? “Strong external headwinds in the form of elevated crude prices and high US bond yields are emboldening bears to build short positions. This is the reason why the market is declining even on days of positive FII and DII buying,” he said. Meanwhile, historical data show that the Nifty has spent at least 150 trading sessions below its 200-DMA on six occasions. The longest such stretch lasted 227 trading sessions, between May 2008 and April 2009, during the global financial crisis triggered by the US subprime mortgage meltdown. The second-longest correction lasted 188 trading sessions on two occasions — between May 2011 and January 2012, and between May and December 2001. Check - TOP GAINERS NSE | TOP LOSERS NSE 
 Shallow correction
 Despite its prolonged duration, the current correction stands out for the relatively small magnitude of the Nifty's decline below its long-term moving average. During the ongoing phase, the index's maximum deficit relative to its 200-DMA has been 11.5 per cent, while its average shortfall has stood at 4.5 per cent. 
 In comparison, among the five other instances when the Nifty spent more than 150 trading sessions below its 200-DMA, the smallest maximum shortfall was 12.6 per cent, recorded during the August 2015-April 2016 correction. The largest was 45.3 per cent during the 2008-09 global financial crisis. The difference is even more pronounced when the duration of deeper declines is considered. During the 2008-09 correction, the Nifty spent 199 of the 227 trading sessions—nearly 88 per cent of the period—at least 10 per cent below its 200-DMA. ALSO READ: NSE, BSE to hold Diwali Muhurat Trading on Nov 8; check timings Similarly, during the 2001 and 1998-99 corrections, the index remained more than 10 per cent below its long-term average for 140 sessions and 123 sessions, respectively, accounting for 74.5 per cent and 78.3 per cent of the respective periods. By contrast, during the current correction, the Nifty has recorded only three trading sessions with a deficit of more than 10 per cent relative to its 200-DMA. Technical view on Nifty From a technical standpoint, the Nifty, said Shrikant Chouhan, Head Equity Research, Kotak Neo, has formed a bearish candle on the daily chart, while the intraday lower-top formation broadly indicates a negative setup. "The 20-day SMA (Simple Moving Average), along with 22,800 and 22,750, would act as key support zones. If it sustains above these, the index could move towards 22,950-23,000. Conversely, selling pressure is likely to increase below 22,750, which could push it towards the 22,650-22,500 zone," he said. Ponmudi R, CEO of Enrich Money, a SEBI-registered online trading and wealth-tech firm, too, remains cautious on the road ahead for the markets and suggests that the Nifty 50 remains under pressure amid persistent selling. The index, he said, maintains a cautious-to-bearish bias, with the near-term direction likely to depend on its ability to sustain above the 22,800 resistance zone while holding the immediate support around 22,600–22,550.
 "On the downside, the 22,600–22,550 range serves as the immediate support zone. A sustained breakdown below 22,500 could intensify selling pressure and drag the index towards the 22,300–22,200 zone," he said.

 Infosys Q2 results preview: Analysts see PAT rising 10%; guidance in focus
 Abhinav Ranjan New Delhi 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 22 2026 | 3:03 PM IST
 Listen to This Article
 Infosys Q2 results preview: Infosys , the country’s second-largest IT services company, is set to announce its Q2FY27 results on Friday (October 23), after market hours. Brokerages expect the company to report revenue growth of around 1.5-1.7 per cent Q-o-Q in constant currency (CC) terms, with margins likely to improve. 
 Brokerages said that the Street will watch for a possible revision in FY27 revenue growth guidance amid demand concerns in some segments. The adjusted PAT in the September quarter may rise by around 10 per cent, while TCV is likely to be in the range of $2.5-3 billion.
 Infosys Q2 results preview by Nuvama 
 Nuvama estimates Infosys' revenue to grow +1.7 per cent Q-o-Q in CC and +1.5 per cent Q-o-Q in USD terms, including 0.5 per cent inorganic and a 0.5 per cent boost from the absence of a provision in the last quarter.
 Ebit may rise by 12.7 per cent Y-o-Y and 3.7 per cent Q-o-Q to ₹10,541 crore, while Ebit margin is likely to expand 40 bps Y-o-Y and 30 bps Q-o-Q to 21.4 per cent.

SIP vs Lumpsum: What should investors do in the current sideways market?
 A lump sum has usually beaten staggered investing, but distributors say a sideways market favours spreading it out. A Systematic Transfer Plan (STP) is the middle path
 Vedant Vichare Mumbai 4 min read Last Updated : Oct 22 2026 | 6:17 PM IST
 Listen to This Article
 Indian retail investors have displayed strong faith in mutual funds despite the ongoing selloff in the Indian stock market, signalling growing maturity. Monthly systematic investment plan (SIP) contributions hit a record ₹32,490 crore in September 2026 . The market, despite these solid inflows, has stalled.
 The BSE barometer Sensex is currently about 14 per cent below its record of about 86,000 points hit in late 2025 and has moved in a range of roughly 71,600 to 74,700 through October. For investors with a lump sum to deploy, such as a bonus or a matured fixed deposit, the question is whether to invest it all now or stagger it.
 Idle cash is uncommon to begin with. Rishit Shah, a Qualified Personal Finance Professional (QPFP) and founder of Vitta Mitra LLP, says investors whose financial planning is in order seldom have extra money lying around. Surplus usually arrives with a hike or a bonus.
 The math vs the risk 
 On average, investing a lump sum has emerged as a better approach.
 From Financial Goals to Regular Investments: How an SIP Calculator Can Help
 HDFC Bank's Puri legacy hard to match; India expensive mkt: Shankar Sharma
 SIP now a long-term bet: Share of investments older than 5 yrs grows to 31%
 Rs 1,322 cr leaves Largecaps in July. Is Investor Money Moving to Midcaps?
 ₹10,000 monthly SIP became ₹36 lakh in 10 yrs: 9 flexi-caps that stood out
 A Vanguard study from 2023 found a lump sum beat a three-month staggered plan about 68 per cent of the time. It used MSCI World Index data from 1976 to 2022 and compared wealth after one year. Equities tend to rise over time, so cash waiting on the sidelines costs returns.
 The gap shows up when markets fall. In the worst 5 per cent of one-year periods, ₹1 lakh invested at once in an all-equity portfolio fell to about ₹83,000, while the same money staggered over three months fell to about ₹86,000.
 Sensex data 
 The table shows what a ₹5,000 monthly SIP in the Sensex would be worth today, against the same total invested as a lump sum on day one.
 Period Total invested SIP value Lumpsum value 1 year ₹60,000 ₹56,358 ₹52,259 5 years ₹3,00,000 ₹3,20,892 ₹3,68,642 10 years ₹6,00,000 ₹9,26,243 ₹15,82,800 20 years ₹12,00,000 ₹34,10,833 ₹68,53,098 
 Lumpsum means the whole amount invested on day one. The SIP spreads the same total over monthly instalments. Source: analysis of BSE Sensex daily closing values to October 21, 2026. Sensex price index, which excludes dividends. Figures are before tax. 
 What it means: over the past year, the SIP lost less because more units were allocated. Over five years and longer, the lump sum finished well ahead, because all of its money was invested from the start in this example. A lump sum does better when markets keep rising, while a SIP, or staggering a lump sum, softens the blow when they fall.
 What mutual fund distributors say: Stagger surplus capital 
 “If you have a long investment horizon, a lump sum investment in equities increases your market exposure, but exposes you to potential losses if the market corrects immediately. Investing in staggered intervals over 3 to 6 months can reduce timing and behavioural risks,” says Rajesh Minocha, CFP, Founder & CEO of Financial Radiance.
 He says a SIP or Systematic Transfer Plan (STP) can work well in volatile, sideways markets, especially when prices dip. But a sideways market is identifiable only in hindsight, he adds, and a lump sum can do better if prices rise sharply or if it lands at the bottom. Nobody knows the bottom until afterwards, so he advises against sitting in cash indefinitely.
 Shah says a sideways market helps SIP investors, who buy at varying prices. For someone with no running SIP, he suggests spreading a lump sum over six to ten months, which he considers enough for most people. He says getting the timing right on a lump sum is difficult for general investors, and the final call depends on risk appetite and how comfortable the investor is with a drawdown.
 The middle path: an STP 
 For a fresh lump sum, distributors commonly suggest an STP. The entire amount goes into a liquid or debt fund, which has returned roughly 6 to 6.5 per cent over the past year. Fixed monthly instalments are then moved into an equity fund over 3 to 10 months.
 For example, take ₹12 lakh in a liquid fund, with ₹2 lakh moved into equity each month for six months, starting on day one. At about 6 per cent, the money waiting in the liquid fund would earn roughly ₹15,000 over the period, before tax.
 Also, each transfer is a redemption from the debt fund and a taxable event. Gains on debt funds bought on or after April 1, 2023 are taxed at the investor’s income slab rate.

Amid ₹48,000 crore FPI retreat, technology stocks are lone bright spot
 Only five sectors attract fresh money; IT leads with ₹2,599 crore
 premium 
 Foreign investors sold shares worth ₹47,955 crore in the first half of October, with IT emerging as the top sector for inflows.
 Kairavi Lukka Mumbai 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 23 2026 | 6:42 AM IST
 Listen to This Article
 Overseas investors stepped up selling in the first half (H1) of October, offloading shares worth ₹47,955 crore across sectors, more than twice the amount they pulled out in the previous fortnight, according to data from the National Securities Depository. Information technology (IT) stocks were the outlier, attracting fresh inflows, even as financial services continued to face selling pressure.
 The outflows in the first fortnight of October were more than double those recorded in the second half of September, when foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) sold shares worth ₹21,745 crore. Of the 24 sectors tracked, only five attracted inflows, while the remaining 19 saw outflows so far this month.
 Financial services recorded the largest outflow at ₹8,634 crore, though this represented less than 0.5 per cent of FPIs’ ₹20 trillion stake in the sector. More telling were the exits from fast-moving consumer goods, automotive, and healthcare, where selling accelerated sharply. FPI equity holdings slipped just 0.3 per cent to ₹65.94 trillion, aided by an 11 per cent jump in the value of their IT holdings. In dollar terms, the portfolio actually grew, supported by a firmer rupee. IT attracted the highest inflows in the first half of October, at ₹2,599 crore.
 “The fortnight reflected a pronounced risk-off stance among foreign investors, with outflows spanning financial, consumption, automotive, and industrial sectors,” said Raj Gaikar, research analyst at Samco Securities. “The isolated inflow into IT suggests selective buying rather than a broad-based shift towards risk assets, highlighting persistent caution in FPI positioning.”
 The buying interest in IT comes amid a strong run in the sector. According to a report by SBI Securities, cumulative net inflows into IT over the past three and a half months stood at ₹9,062 crore. The Nifty IT index rose 10.88 per cent in H1 of October, appreciably outperforming the benchmark Nifty index, which gained 1.67 per cent over the same period, said SBI Securities’ note. 
 “The Nifty IT index has negated its lower-low, lower-high structure on the daily time frame and moved above its previous major swing-high zone of 31,900–32,000, closing higher. Sustaining above this zone will be crucial for the index to extend its upward momentum in the near term,” the report noted. 
 Services also continued to attract foreign investor interest. SBI Securities said that, barring April, the sector had recorded inflows in every other month of the current financial year. “India’s Services Purchasing Managers’ Index rose to 55.2 in September 2026, up from 54.1 in August. A reading above 50 indicates expansion in the services sector,” the report said.
 The sectoral picture also shifted between the second half of September and H1 of October. FPIs increased their purchases of chemicals, IT, and media, entertainment and publication stocks compared with the previous fortnight.
 Several sectors also shifted from net inflows in the latter half of September to net outflows in October so far.
 Healthcare saw outflows of ₹5,497 crore in H1 of October, the highest since April, when the sector recorded outflows of ₹7,223 crore, according to the SBI Securities report. The report added that the healthcare index broke below the neckline of a triple-top pattern at the beginning of October and has slipped below key short- and long-term moving averages.

Eternal eyes faster Blinkit expansion as margins and order values grow
 Eternal plans to accelerate Blinkit's store rollout to 3,500 outlets by FY27-end, backed by strong order growth, while stable food delivery margins and AI bets shape its outlook.
 premium 
 Eternal reported strong Q2FY27 revenue growth, driven by Blinkit's expansion and steady performance in Zomato's food delivery business.
 Devangshu Datta New Delhi 5 min read Last Updated : Oct 23 2026 | 7:25 AM IST
 Listen to This Article
 Eternal delivered fairly positive Q2FY27 results and confident commentary. The food delivery (FD) business saw stable margins and growth rates at the higher end of consensus estimates. Quick commerce (QC) has high competitive intensity and Blinkit is accelerating its network rollout. Hyperpure and District look to be on promising trajectories. The company is also making a potentially high-reward gamble in AI development. It doesn’t think agentic commerce is a threat as yet.
 Eternal reported Q2FY27 net revenue of Rs 24,100 crore, up 19.4 per cent quarter-on-quarter (QoQ) and 77.6 per cent year-on-year (YoY). The FD net order value (NOV) was Rs 11,450 crore, and Blinkit NOV was Rs 20,900 crore, up 79.3 per cent YoY. In FD (Zomato), the ratio of adjusted earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (Ebitda) to NOV decreased 10 basis points QoQ to 5.5 per cent.
 Blinkit reported a contribution margin of 5.3 per cent, the same as in Q1FY27, and an adjusted Ebitda margin of 0.9 per cent. Net profit stood at Rs 125 crore, up 92.3 per cent YoY. Consolidated Ebitda was Rs 750 crore, lower than consensus estimates. Net profit was also pulled down by a higher effective tax rate (61 per cent) as all tax shields from carried-forward losses were exhausted. Going forward, the standalone entity’s profits will be taxed at the full rate.
 The FD margin is likely to be more or less stable for the next two financial years, with any incremental profits being reinvested. Growth will be the priority. In its guidance, Eternal has a long-term target of over 20 per cent annual NOV growth, despite competitive intensity.
 In QC, Blinkit’s expansion will accelerate. NOV grew 79.3 per cent YoY in Q2, and growth is expected to accelerate further in Q3 as store expansion ramps up. Blinkit is still the sector leader despite intense competition, due to intelligent assortment, category breadth and good execution. The FY27-end store target has been raised to 3,500 from 3,000 earlier, with the next target of 5,000 by FY28-end.
 Improving store payback in smaller geographies and a “more predictable” competitive environment are cited as key factors behind the acceleration in rollout. Blinkit beat its 60 per cent annual NOV growth guidance over the last three-year period. Profitability in larger, mature markets will support store expansion, as mature cities generate adjusted Ebitda margins of over 5 per cent. Cities accounting for 70 per cent of NOV are adjusted Ebitda-positive, and 96 per cent of NOV is contribution-positive. 
 District is on track to achieve adjusted Ebitda breakeven within four to six quarters from January 2026 and has guided for Rs 28,000 crore in NOV and Rs 1,400 crore in adjusted Ebitda by FY30.
 Hyperpure revenue was up 22.7 per cent YoY, with the restaurant count at 85,000, up from 62,000 at Q1FY27-end. The adjusted Ebitda margin has turned positive, at 0.9 per cent from -0.5 per cent a year ago.
 Eternal’s AI development product, Dark.ai, is an early-stage investment in privacy-focused AI. Its models are hosted on Eternal’s infrastructure, with end-to-end encryption and user-controlled encrypted memory. The product targets power users who require privacy for sensitive work. The management describes this as an early-stage opportunity, with monetisation potential and investment requirements yet to be clearly assessed.
 At first glance, it appears to be a big diversification from the core businesses, but Eternal requires AI to manage all of its digital business lines. At this point, the costs and investment aren't substantial, so it's best described as a wild card. Management calls it a "zero-one" (all or nothing) bet, which can scale up if it works or else be shut down. Nugget (Enterprise AI) is another similar zero-one bet.
 The management commentary also discussed the possible impact of agentic commerce, which may lead to disintermediation. Platforms controlling fulfilment and supply-chain infrastructure may be better positioned than pure intermediaries in the delivery business. Management expects Zomato and Blinkit to remain relatively resilient to agentic commerce, given their integrated delivery and inventory networks. District faces higher exposure.
 It also expects in-app AI interfaces to address repeat orders, while browsing-led search and discovery are crucial for FD.
 The (pre-tax) business dynamics for Zomato, Blinkit, District and Hyperpure remain good despite strong competition. FD is an effective duopoly, but competitive intensity is up since new entrants are trying to establish a foothold. Blinkit is in a much more crowded market. FD is profitable, but tax incidence is up. Blinkit is growing both NOV and margins.
 A Hyperpure turnaround and breakeven would probably lead to a higher valuation multiple for the company, and the same applies to District. Post-tax profitability may lead to earnings estimates being shaved. The Dark.ai and Nugget plays are imponderables. There’s cash on the balance sheet to fund them if they look like paying off. Investors will hope Eternal has not underestimated agentic commerce.

docs.title: Indian Hotels surges 5%: Brokerages see 15% upside on 700-hotel portfolio target by FY27
docs.text: The Indian Hotels Company share price surged over 5% in early trade today, October 22. The shares are in focus after it posted firm results for the second quarter of financial year 2027 (Q2FY27). Several global and domestic brokerages have retained their ‘Buy’ recommendations on the stock and have projected positive outlooks. Indian Hotels Q2 earnings The Indian Hotels Company reported a net profit of Rs 380 crore for the September quarter, up 19.5% year-on-year (YoY). Its revenue from operations rose 22% to Rs 2,484 crore from Rs 2,041 crore a year ago. The company’s EBITDA increased nearly 24% to Rs 706 crore. However, EBITDA margin contracted to 19.95% from 27.9% a year earlier. ALSO READBeyond Titan and Kalyan: The smallcaps supplying India’s jewellery giants Jefferies on Indian Hotels: MICE opportunities Global investment bank Jefferies has retained its ‘Buy’ rating on the stock and has a target price of Rs 900. This implies an upside of 15% from the current price of Rs 782 apiece. Jefferies has raised its FY27 EBITDA/EPS estimate for the company by 1.2-1.5%, and factors in the consolidation of Oriental Hotels from FY28. It raised its FY28/FY29 EBITDA/PAT by around 4.5%. The company raised its revenue growth guidance for FY27 to 15-17% from 12-14%, including a 17-19% growth in the hotel segment. “Asset management continues to drive growth and value creation, with major property upgrades translating into stronger pricing power,” Jefferies said. Indian Hotels targets to open 50 new hotels in FY27, including 30 in the second half of the year. Its pipeline remains capital-light, with 94% of hotels under this model and 81% under management contracts. The company is now looking at a portfolio target of 700 hotels by the end of FY27 compared to the earlier forecast of FY30. “The opportunity in social MICE (Meetings, Incentives, Conferences, and Exhibitions) remains significant in next year, with 95 wedding dates in CY27 versus a typical 60-65, providing a sustained demand tailwind,” Jefferies added. Motilal Oswal on Indian Hotels: Healthy traction in core ops Motilal Oswal also maintained its ‘Buy’ rating on the stock, with a target price of Rs 870, implying an upside of over 11% from the current price. The brokerage expects the company to continue to post strong results. It sees a revenue growth of 14% on a compounded annual growth rate (CAGR) basis over FY26 to FY28. Motilal expects EBITDA and adjusted profit after tax to rise 15% and 19% CAGR over the same period, respectively. “We remain optimistic on IH’s growth outlook despite near-term geopolitical and macroeconomic uncertainties, led by healthy traction in the core business as well as new and reimagined businesses,” it said. The brokerage expects the momentum to be driven by strong room addition pipeline in owned hotels, strategic acquisitions, and continued favourable demand-supply dynamics. Nomura on Indian Hotels: Earnings estimates raised The Japanese brokerage firm also retained its ‘Buy’ call on the stock. Nomura raised its target price for the stock by 2% to Rs 850, implying an upside of around 9% from the current price. ALSO READZomato: Agentic AI fear overblown? Brokerages reaffirm ‘Buy’ with up to 38% upside The brokerage has raised several of its projections for the company, including revenue per available room (Revpar) and EBITDA margin. Nomura raised FY27 Revpar growth to 15% from 10%, and standalone EBITDA margin to 46% from 44%. “Our revised estimates also assume weaker than expected performance from Taj Sats/ international subsidiaries,” it said. It expects standalone revenue growth of 17-18% in the second half of FY27 and EBITDA growth of 20%. “This would lead to FY27F standalone EBITDA growing ~27% y-y. As we expect some margin dilution from TajSats/ International subsidiaries, we estimate FY27F consolidated EBITDA to grow ~20% y-y. For FY28F, we estimate consolidated EBITDA to grow ~15% y-y, led by standalone growth of 15-16% y-y as we expect high-single-digit samestore-sales growth, management fee growth and Oriental Hotel consolidation,” the brokerage said. docs.title: Zomato: Agentic AI fear overblown? Brokerages reaffirm ‘Buy’ with up to 38% upside
docs.text: The Eternal share price is in focus after the company posted its quarterly results on Wednesday. Several brokerages have retained their ‘Buy’ calls on the stock and some have even raised their target prices. The Zomato and Blinkit operator’s execution remains on track, and the quick commerce business continues to accelerate. The impact from agentic commerce is seen limited, though it remains vigilant. Here is what brokerages are saying about the company’s performance and outlook: Jefferies on Zomato: Unfazed by agentic commerce Global investment bank Jefferies has a ‘Buy’ rating on Zomato, and has raised its target price by around 4% to Rs 430 apiece. This implies an upside of nearly 38% from the stock’s current price of Rs 312.4 apiece. Jefferies raised the FY27-FY29 adjusted EBITDA view by 5-8%. ALSO READBeyond Titan and Kalyan: The smallcaps supplying India’s jewellery giants “Eternal unveiled dark.ai, a privacy-focused AI application built on open-source models. Through this, the company uses fine-tuned frontier open-weight models that run on its own infra. 'End-to-end encryption' is the key promise, i.e., no one can read user conversations. Mgmt highlighted it as 'zero to one' bet. Costs are currently not meaningful; if scaled, investment would mainly be in hardware/compute,” it said. Jefferies said the company’s management remains unfazed by agentic commerce and has a strong point of view. The agentic commerce model is not seen as a “material threat” to the Zomato and Blinkit business model, including margins. “.agents could instead drive 'winner-takes-all' outcomes toward execution leaders & strengthen supply chain moats. Agentic adoption in India remains negligible; Blinkit is agentfriendly & investing in relevant protocols, while Zomato is experimenting with conversational ordering, though users prefer browsing,” Jefferies added. Nomura on Eternal: Quick commerce margins seen stable The brokerage retained its ‘Buy’ rating on the stock and has a target price of Rs 350. This indicates an upside of 12% from the stock’s current price of Rs 312.4 apiece. Eternal’s net order value (NOV) has grown steadily, and the number of monthly transacting users (MTU) has also improved. The company noted that competition remains intense in the food delivery business, and that it intends to keep its margin stable and reinvest higher margins into growth. Nomura has lowered its adjusted EBITDA margin view for the food delivery business by 20 basis points for FY27 and 50 bps for FY28. The brokerage expects NOV to grow 17% year-on-year (YoY) in FY27 and 22% in FY28. “Blinkit expects to rapidly add new dark stores especially in Tier-2 and lower cites to gain a first mover advantage, targeting a store count of 3,500 by FY27E-end (vs 3,000 earlier) and 5,000 by FY28E. In the near term, store openings will keep margins stable while longer term margin improvement will be driven by scale, as per Blinkit,” the brokerage said. Nomura flagged slower-than-expected profitability improvement in quick commerce due to competition and a slowdown of the food delivery business as the key risks. Motilal Oswal on Eternal: Blinkit offers long growth runway The brokerage retained its ‘Buy’ rating on the stock, and has a price target of Rs 420. This implies an upside of 34% from the current price. “Blinkit’s expansion to accelerate, with NOV growth expected to pick up: NOV grew 79.3% YoY in 2Q, and growth is expected to pick up from 3Q as new stores come online and ramp up. Despite intense competition, Blinkit’s assortment intelligence, category breadth and execution capabilities are supporting customer acquisition and store paybacks,” Motilal Oswal said. ALSO READIndian IT stocks rally 12% in a week – Is the turnaround sustainable? The brokerage said Eternal’s food delivery business is stable, while Blinkit offers a long runway to participate in the structural shift in retail, grocery, and e-commerce. Motilal Oswal expects the company to report PAT margins of 0.8% and 1.4% for FY27 and FY28, respectively. It continues to factor in management's long-term growth trajectory of over 60% NOV growth for the quick commerce business, along with gradual margin expansion through store maturity and operating leverage. Eternal: Good growth, quick commerce has more potential The Zomato operator posted robust results for the September quarter. Its execution remains on track and the quick commerce business is expected to accelerate, with more dark store additions in the pipeline. The impact from agentic commerce is seen limited, though the company remains vigilant.
