docs.title: No guarantee of a reliable partnership
docs.text: Transactionalism and flattery rank high on the US-India-Russia relationships. Accompanied by businessmen, Secretary of State Marco Rubio visited Mumbai and Jamnagar from October 20-22 . Prior to his trip, Rubio even referred to India as an “important ally”. That was better than being lambasted as a hellhole by President Donald Trump less than six months ago. As US diesel prices rose to record highs, largely because of America’s inability to defeat Iran since it invaded that country with Israel in March, Trump decided that America would buy Russian diesel with the intent of easing diesel prices to improve the Republicans’ chances of winning November’s mid-term elections. Branding India anew as “a refining superpower”, Rubio travelled to Jamnagar, in Prime Minister Modi’s home state of Gujarat, to tour Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries oil refinery complex, which is the world’s largest. An old buyer of Venezuelan oil, Ambani was quick to cultivate ties with the Trump administration by investing in the first new refinery project in the US in 50 years, and by purchasing more Venezuelan oil barrels after last January’s Trumpian coup in Venezuela. ALSO READThe CEO deserves a shower at 40,000 ft Rubio even showed understanding of India’s decision to continue purchasing Russian oil by voicing appreciation of India’s difficulties in pivoting from Russian imports “in a day”. Essentially, Rubio engaged with India’s largest concentration of economic power—one which led Elon Musk to sarcastically label Ambani as the prime minister and “real boss” of India. Two preferences of the Trumpian establishment are clear. First, they signify that although corporate financiers might compete with each other, they are simultaneously the prime movers and keystone of international relations. Whether that signals Washington’s disregard of India’s aspiration to be treated as a favoured international partner, despite their Comprehensive Global Strategic Partnership, is uncertain. Second, Washington doesn’t want to be dependent on any single country, and Rubio advised India to diversify its oil suppliers. India should buy less from Russia, which currently provides 50% of its oil imports, and buy more Venezuelan and American oil. ALSO READPower before bytes From a different angle, External Affairs Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar voiced the expectation that India’s partners should show “zero tolerance” for global terrorism—implying Pakistani-trained and -sponsored terrorists—when he met Rubio. But Delhi should realise that the US will use Pakistan to project its aims in West Asia—as it has since the Cold War—regardless of India’s more recent talk of anti-terrorism. And Trump claimed that his mediation staved off an Indo-Pak war in 2025—which India denied. Moreover, given that Pakistan and China are close partners, at a time when Trump is cultivating Beijing, Islamabad gains a further advantage in Washington. On trade, Rubio’s expectation that a deal was in the offing also came as a surprise. As recently as on October 1, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer affirmed that a bilateral trade deal between the US and India was “not imminent”, although negotiations were in their final phase. And Delhi has been fed up that Washington’s sole criteria to reduce India’s $58-billion trade surplus, which has prevailed over many years, is apparently to make up “for all that they’ve lost over these years”. Trump, however, underlined “the power that we have with us”, while Jaishankar pointed to America’s unpredictable trade policies. Now, the US expects trade with India to hit a record high on $500 billion—compared to $ 240 billion at present—within three years, and is ready to skip unresolved matters in the final deal. Washington has taken into account an anticipated India-US trade deal to waive tariffs on Delhi’s Russian oil purchases. India’s ability to turn crude oil into diesel could be particularly valuable in improving their trade ties. Commercial and strategic interests are intertwined. Militarily, America is not one of India’s three top arms retailers. Washington will not give the F-35 aircraft or co-produce it with India because Delhi retains close military ties with Moscow. India has bought the S-400 Triumf air defence system and is considering buying the SU-57. Turkey, a NATO ally, also bought the S-400, which resulted in Trump 1.0’s decision to cancel its F-35 contract in 2019. Allies and the weapons they receive do matter to Trump, although he wants them to pay more for their defence against Russia or China. America is within its rights to regulate immigration or what Jaishankar euphemistically referred to as people-to-people contacts in Mumbai. Although new rules have been introduced to curb Indians and foreigners from residing in the US, Rubio claims they do not target India. But the debate over the regulation of immigration is tied to Trump administration’s MAGA nativism, and its ideas of racial supremacy. Those rules continue to come into conflict with Delhi’s analogous talk about India’s civilisational greatness and claim to be the world teacher. At another level, India’s response to Vice President JD Vance’s insult to “indentured” Indian workers in America suggests that immigration has become a social and political quarrel between Delhi and Washington, partly because Indians have long perceived Indo-Americans as having enhanced their global stature, partly because America is the favourite emigration destination for Indians—but not vice-versa. Their remittances account for nearly 2% of India’s GDP. This is slightly more than Delhi’s spending on health for more than a billion citizens. India’s dependence on the US stems from its slow progress, and it will not vanish if the latter buys diesel from Ambani. Prosperous countries make the best allies, said Trump during his first term. Even then, as America’s current ties with its West European allies reveal, prosperity alone is no guarantee of trust between allies and

docs.title: JM Financial sees 49% upside in this retail stock under Rs 150 on festive demand
docs.text: Every shopkeeper knows this moment. The lights are up, the shelves are stocked, and the festival rush is due any day. Then the calendar shifts, and the crowd turns up weeks later. Something similar played out at a large Indian retail chain this quarter. Sales rose, but profits grew much slower than expected. So was this a real slowdown, or just bad timing? For investors tracking stocks under Rs 150, the key question is whether a temporary slowdown could give way to stronger growth in the coming months. The stock in focus is Vishal Mega Mart (VMM). According to JM Financial, the retailer’s July-September quarter performance fell short of expectations, mainly because festive demand moved into the October-December quarter. The brokerage has retained its ‘Buy’ rating and an unchanged target price of Rs 134, implying an upside potential of around 49% from the reference price used in its report. Let's take a look at why the brokerage house is bullish on this stock and the rationale behind the investment call - Why did Vishal Mega Mart miss expectations? Vishal Mega Mart reported revenue of Rs 3,400 crore in the Q2FY27, up 14% year-on-year. However, EBITDA increased by just 4.4% to Rs 410 crore. The EBITDA margin fell 111 basis points to 12.1%. ALSO READ142.1% profit growth: Why Hindustan Zinc still trades near its 52-week low According to JM Financial, EBITDA was 8% below its estimate, while profit after tax (PAT) missed expectations by 12%. Net profit rose 3.7% year-on-year to Rs 160 crore. The timing of festivals was a key factor. Navratri, Durga Puja and Dussehra shifted into the third quarter, affecting demand for clothing during the July-September period. Apparel sales grew 9.5%, compared with 18.2% growth in fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG). Vishal Mega Mart: More stores, but are they generating enough sales Opening new stores can increase revenue, but profitability also depends on how much each store sells and the cost of running it. Vishal Mega Mart’s store network expanded 13.7% year-on-year to 844 outlets. Same-store sales growth (SSSG) stood at 5.4%. JM Financial said this growth would have been around 9% after adjusting for the festive shift. However, revenue per square foot increased only 2.8%, while retail operating costs per square foot rose 5.7%. Employee costs per square foot climbed 14.2%. As a result, pre-Ind AS EBITDA per square foot declined 8.7% year-on-year. The brokerage believes the earnings shortfall is largely timing-related rather than evidence of a sustained slowdown. Vishal Mega Mart: Can the festive quarter change the picture? The next quarter will be important. Management reported a strong start to the festive season and expects double-digit same-store sales growth in the Q3FY27. The company also expects gross margins to remain stable in the second half, despite elevated raw material prices. It has limited price increases to higher-priced products and does not currently plan further hikes. Management is targeting more than 100 store additions annually and expects annual EBITDA margin improvement of around 30 basis points. Its new apparel format, Belong & Co., has also recorded early customer traction. ALSO READIndia’s warship boom has a catch: Why Goldman Sachs is betting against Mazagon Dock, GRSE What is JM Financial’s view on Vishal Mega? JM Financial has reduced its earnings estimates for financial years 2026-27 to 2028-29 by 2-3% to account for weaker first-half performance and higher operating costs. However, it has maintained its ‘Buy’ rating and target price of Rs 134. The retailer’s cash position remains another factor to watch. It generated Rs 520 crore in free cash flow before Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS) adjustments during the first half and reported net cash of Rs 2,330 crore. docs.title: 6 ‘Buy’ recommendations by Nomura, with up to 33% upside potential
docs.text: Nomura has maintained ‘Buy’ ratings on a range of Indian stocks across financial services, cement, real estate and aviation, with its latest research pointing to potential gains of up to 33%. Bajaj Finance, Piramal Finance and UltraTech Cement lead the list, supported by expectations of loan growth, improving asset quality, resilient cement demand and better pricing. The brokerage’s reports published between October 17 and 20 also favour ICICI Bank, Oberoi Realty and InterGlobe Aviation. The investment cases differ, with lenders banking on growth and profitability, real estate companies relying on project execution and recurring income, and the cement maker looking for price increases to offset higher fuel costs. Nomura’s six ‘Buy’ stocks with the highest upside StockNomura ratingTarget priceUpside potentialBajaj Finance‘Buy’Rs 1,27032.7%Piramal Finance‘Buy’Rs 2,55030.8%UltraTech Cement‘Buy’Rs 13,70028.6%InterGlobe Aviation‘Buy’Rs 6,00025.6%Oberoi Realty‘Buy’Rs 2,09024.7%ICICI Bank‘Buy’Rs 1,74024.6% Source: Nomura research reports published between October 17 and 20, 2026. Upside figures are as stated in the respective reports. Nomura on Bajaj Finance: ‘Buy’ Nomura retained its ‘Buy’ rating on Bajaj Finance after the company reported September-quarter profit growth in line with the brokerage’s estimate. It raised its full-year loan growth guidance, while flagging some pressure on net interest margins from higher interest rates. The brokerage expects growth across lending segments to remain healthy, with newer businesses such as gold loans adding to the portfolio. It expects the company to deliver a return on assets of 4.2% and return on equity of 19.9% over FY28-FY29. Nomura has set a target price of Rs 1,270 for Bajaj Finance, implying an upside potential of 32.7%. However, global investment bank Jefferies is bullish on KEI Industries. docs.text: India’s expanding metro network is creating fresh opportunities for railway rolling stock manufacturers. As cities invest in new metro corridors and additional trains, demand for domestically manufactured metro coaches could gain momentum. The latest opportunity comes from Hyderabad. On 16 October 2026, the Delhi Metro Rail Corporation (DMRC) floated a tender worth Rs 923.62 crore for 60 metro coaches. The contract includes design, manufacturing, supply, commissioning and 15 years of comprehensive maintenance. The deadline for submitting bids is 13 January 2027. However, not every railway company is positioned to benefit directly. Metro coach manufacturing requires specialised production facilities, technical expertise and a proven execution record. Companies with established capabilities and completed deliveries may be better placed to compete for such contracts. We identified two Indian-listed companies with operational metro coach manufacturing facilities, successful delivery records and existing order pipelines. While the Hyderabad tender represents a potential opportunity rather than a confirmed order, both companies offer direct exposure to India's growing metro rolling stock market. Let's examine their manufacturing capabilities, existing contracts and financial performance to understand how they are positioned for the next phase of metro expansion. The company crossed the 2,100-coach manufacturing milestone in May 2025. Its portfolio includes driverless metro trains equipped with Grade of Automation 4 (GoA4) technology. This manufacturing track record and completed deliveries support its inclusion among companies positioned to benefit from upcoming metro tenders. Metro coaches currently have an indigenisation level of around 65%, according to the company's FY26 annual report. BEML is working to increase domestic sourcing further. Why Rail & Metro Commands 65% of BEML’s Orders but Only 24% of Revenue Rail & Metro represented 65% of BEML's order book in August 2026, against a 24% contribution to FY26 revenue. Management expects to deliver 20–25 trains to Bengaluru Metro during FY27. The company is also pursuing six metro tenders across Chennai, Delhi, Uttar Pradesh, Pune-Nagpur and Mumbai. The September quarter brought further railway orders. BEML secured a contract exceeding Rs 5,400 crore from NHSRCL for high-speed rolling stock and maintenance on the Mumbai-Ahmedabad corridor. It also received a Rs 180.6 crore order for additional Vande Bharat Sleeper trainsets. These contracts are separate from metro manufacturing but add to its railway order pipeline. BEML’s Bhopal Expansion: An 18-Month Timeline With Construction Yet to Begin BEML plans to increase rail coach manufacturing capacity from approximately 250 to 350–400 units annually. Its proposed BRAHMA facility near Bhopal will support this expansion. According to the August earnings-call transcript, civil construction had yet to begin. Management expects the first equipment to roll out 18 months after construction starts. Exports offer another growth avenue. BEML secured its first metro rolling stock export contract worth Rs 550 crore for Africa. It is also pursuing two overseas metro opportunities estimated at Rs 15,000 crore combined. In FY26, revenue increased 8.2% year-on-year (YoY) to Rs 4,351 crore. However, net profit declined 50% to Rs 147 crore. The annual report attributed pressure on profitability partly to provisions exceeding Rs 257 crore, including cost escalation and foreign exchange impacts on metro contracts. BEML is yet to declare its Q2FY27 financial results. Valuations remain demanding. EV/EBITDA stands at 42.3 times, against a historical median of 29 times and peer multiple of 19.7 times. Return on capital employed (ROCE) of 7.7% and return on equity (ROE) of 4.5% indicate modest capital efficiency. Timely execution, improved margins and working capital management remain important as the order pipeline expands. Its operating manufacturing facility at Uttarpara, completed metro deliveries and contracts across Bengaluru, Ahmedabad, Surat and Mumbai support its inclusion among listed companies positioned to benefit from rising metro coach demand. docs.title: Beyond Titan and Kalyan: The smallcaps supplying India’s jewellery giants
docs.text: India’s B2B jewellery manufacturers are catching market attention. Sky Gold has surged around 200% in 2026 so far. Meanwhile, other B2B jewellery manufacturers have also seen sharp gains. Shringar House of Mangalsutra rose nearly 50% in October till date, while Shanti Gold gained 109.5% in 2026 so far. The trend points to growing interest in companies that manufacture jewellery for retail chains rather than sell directly to consumers. The difference lies in the business model. B2C jewellers like Titan Company and Kalyan Jewellers need showrooms, retail staff and marketing to reach customers. B2B manufacturers, on the other hand, can grow by supplying multiple jewellery retailers. They can focus on production, design and order execution without having to build an extensive retail network. The timing also matters. Organised jewellers are projected to increase their share of India’s jewellery market from 35.2% in CY23 to 59.7% by CY29. As these retailers open more stores and refresh their collections, their need for reliable manufacturing partners could rise. FE Stock Insights on WhatsApPGet instant alerts on high-conviction investment themes and fundamental deep dives—direct from Financial Express.Join now For B2B jewellery manufacturers, this offers an opportunity to benefit from the expansion of organised retail without bearing the full cost of running consumer-facing stores. Against this backdrop, let’s look at three lesser-known small-cap jewellery companies that could benefit from this shift. #1 Shanti Gold: Doubling Capacity to Feed India's Mega-Retailers Shanti Gold International (market cap: ₹3,000 crore) is an Indian B2B gold jewellery manufacturer serving large organised retail chains, regional retailers, and international markets. It specialises in Cubic Zirconia (CZ) casting and studded gold jewellery (70-75% of its product sales mix) and plain gold jewellery (25-30%). Order-Book Expansion: Tapping North India and High-Margin Turkish Designs The company is now expanding into high-volume machine-made plain gold jewellery and value-added categories such as Turkish and designer jewellery. Shanti Gold serves major national and regional brands including Kalyan Jewellers, Joyalukkas, Lalithaa Jewellery and Bhima Jewellers. Shanti Gold has an installed capacity of 6,700 kg per annum after commissioning an additional 4,000 kg per annum. The company is adding another 1,200 kg of annual capacity, bringing total capacity to 7,900 kg per annum once the Jaipur facility becomes operational. The company expects to bring this capacity online by December 2026. It is scaling value-added sub-categories such as Turkish jewellery and introducing high-volume machine-made plain gold jewellery. Management is also expanding into North Indian markets where it does not yet have access. Shanti Gold delivered strong Q1FY27 performance. Sales volume reached 522.1 kg, up 61.6% year-on-year from 323.0 kg in Q1 FY26. Deeper engagement with existing organised retail clients, the rollout of new designs and entry into new domestic markets such as Northern India supported growth. As a result, revenue from operations jumped 144.7% to ₹716.38 crore. Net profit doubled to ₹50 crore. Guidance vs Delivery: Can 30-40% Volume Run-Rate Sustain 8% EBITDA Margins? Looking ahead, the management estimates revenue of ₹3,500 crore in FY27, comprising 50-60% value growth and 30-40% volume growth. Management expects the 30-40% volume growth trajectory to be sustainable over the next 3 to 4 years. Management expects sustainable EBITDA margins to settle in the 7.5-8.0% range. Shanti Gold Share Price #2 Utssav CZ Gold Jewels: High Margins and Global Ambitions at a Premium P/E Utssav CZ Gold Jewels (market cap: ₹2,350 crore) is a well-known Indian B2B jewellery manufacturing company. The company specialises in lightweight CZ gold jewellery, rose gold jewellery, plain gold casting and diamond jewellery. Its product portfolio includes a design library of over 70,000 and 300,000 CAD creations. ALSO READTitan’s smaller rivals match its growth—at 41%–85% P/E discounts The company operates across 23 Indian states and two Union Territories and serves a network of 430+ retailers and distributors. Utssav maintains strong long-term relationships with an 85%+ repeat business rate, while onboarding 112 new B2B clients in FY26 alone. It operates a 100% integrated in-house manufacturing process. Capex Runway: Targeting 7,500-Kg Capacity as Peak Utilization Hits 90% The company currently has an installed capacity of 2,000 to 2,500 kg per annum. Current capacity utilisation averages 65% and reaches up to 90% during peak festive/wedding seasons. Utssav is looking for a new, larger plant to scale total annual production capacity to 6,000-7,500 kg. The company is targeting to onboard 100-200 new B2B clients in FY27. The company expects 60% revenue growth and 35-40% volume growth in FY27. Management expects sustainable long-term EBITDA margins of 7-8% and net profit margins of 4-4.5%. Management aims to grow annual revenue to ₹4,000-5,000 crore by 2030. Utssav is expanding into natural diamond and lab-grown diamond to diversify revenues and tap emerging segments. The Dubai & Lab-Grown Gateway: Mapping the ₹5,000-Crore FY30 Ambition Management aims to increase annual revenue from the diamond segment to more than ₹200 crore within 2 to 3 years (currently 2%). The company is also establishing a presence in Dubai, a global gold trading hub. Management expects the export share of revenue to jump from 1-2% to 10-20%. It is also expanding into Singapore, Malaysia, Australia and the US. The company reports half-yearly financial results (for periods ending September and March). The company delivered significant top-line and bottom-line growth during FY26. Revenue from operations increased 78.7% year-on-year to ₹1,157.5 crore. EBITDA increased 132.3% to ₹93.7 crore, while margins expanded 187 bps to 8.1%. Net profit grew 135.7% to ₹59 crore. Utssav CZ Share Price

docs.title: Vijay Kedia’s latest bets: Rs 73 cr in 2 smallcaps with surging profits
docs.text: Vijay Kedia Latest Investments: Decoding His 2026 SME Portfolio Picks The September 2026 shareholding filings of SME companies, which report only twice a year, have finally put two of Vijay Kedia's newer positions on record. Kedia Securities, his investment firm, now shows up with 8.06% of Sattrix Information Security, a cybersecurity company listed on the BSE SME platform. In Iware Supplychain Services, a logistics company listed on NSE Emerge, Kedia and his firm together hold 10.35%. The two stakes were worth about Rs 73 cr at the close on 21st October 2026. That is roughly 5% of the Rs 1,357 cr he publicly holds across 24 stocks. Small money for Kedia, but a loud signal. He is the investor behind the SMILE framework: small in size, medium in experience, large in aspiration and extra-large in market potential. SME stocks are where that idea gets tested hardest. Neither stake was built the usual way, through steady buying in the market. One came through a share swap. The other began with a preferential allotment. And what both companies have told the exchanges in the past few weeks is more useful than the price Kedia paid. A word of caution before we go deeper. These are both SME stocks and trade in large lots, report results only twice a year and can be hard to exit when the mood turns. Investors should treat them as risky bets and size them accordingly. Let us dive in. FE Stock Insights on WhatsApPGet instant alerts on high-conviction investment themes and fundamental deep dives—direct from Financial Express.Join now #1 Sattrix Information Security: Vijay Kedia’s SME Cybersecurity Position Incorporated in 2013, Sattrix Information Security builds and runs cybersecurity systems for companies in India, the US and the UAE. Its work covers round-the-clock security monitoring, software licences, implementation and managed security services. The company listed on the BSE SME platform in June 2024 at an issue price of Rs 121. At Rs 304.75 on 21st October 2026, the stock trades at about 2.5 times that price, with a market cap of about Rs 346 cr. The Share Swap Mechanics: What Kedia’s 8% Equity Stake Actually Cost In February 2026, Sattrix bought 100% of Sattrix Software Solutions, an unlisted firm run by the same promoters, for Rs 157.83 cr. It paid in its own stock, issuing 45,48,379 new shares at Rs 347 each, as per its BSE filings. Kedia Securities was a shareholder in the unlisted firm and received 9,14,906 Sattrix shares in the swap. What is new is that the stake now appears in the September 2026 shareholding pattern. At Rs 304.75, that holding is valued at about Rs 27.9 cr, against roughly Rs 31.7 cr at the swap price. Valuation Realities: Decoding the 52x Sales Multiple in the Sattrix Acquisition The firm Sattrix bought had a turnover of just Rs 3.02 cr in FY25, as per the company's disclosure to BSE. The price works out to about 52 times sales. Promoters sat on both sides of the deal and received most of the new shares, lifting their stake from 73.53% to 74.96%. The company has said the deal was done at arm's length and backed by an independent valuation. Most of that price now sits on the balance sheet. Fixed assets jumped from Rs 7.44 cr in FY25 to Rs 163.78 cr in FY26. That is why book value looks large at Rs 179 a share, and why return on capital employed slid to 9.6% from 23.6% a year earlier. Sattrix FY26 Earnings Analysis: Revenue Acceleration Meets Margin Compression Financial YearFY21FY22FY23FY24FY25FY265Y CAGRSales (Rs cr)21.1222.9436.5940.3744.6360.8324%EBITDA (Rs cr)3.302.664.902.516.8912.4730%Net Profit (Rs cr)1.942.144.001.804.058.0833%Source: Screener.in EBITDA here refers to operating profit before other income. FY26 was the company's best year by a distance. Sales rose 36% and profit roughly doubled. The second half did the heavy lifting, with operating margin at 27.7% against 12.1% in the first half. That is the half in which the acquired business joined the books. The cash story is weaker. Debtor days rose to 234 from 177 a year earlier, which means customers are taking about eight months to pay. Cash from operations was just Rs 2.23 cr in FY26, against operating profit of Rs 12.47 cr. Cybersecurity Order Book Dynamics: Navigating the Volatility in Monthly Disclosures Sattrix files monthly order updates with BSE, and they swing hard. Orders came to Rs 12.45 cr in June and Rs 18.17 cr in August. In between, it won a three-year Rs 9.3 cr order from a public sector bank and a one-year Rs 17.35 cr contract from a private bank. September brought orders of only about Rs 47.5 lakh. The filings themselves have needed fixing. In April, the company rectified a disclosure on a Rs 9.30 cr bank contract. It later corrected its June order figure. On 7th October, it withdrew a press release on September orders that it said was issued by mistake, then filed a revised one. Small slips, perhaps, but monthly updates are much of what SME investors have to go on. Sattrix Valuation Metrics: Assessing the 42x PE Ratio Against Sector Averages The stock trades at a PE of about 42x and the industry median currently is 24x. A 10-year median PE comparison is not possible here as Sattrix has been listed for under two and a half years. The share price is about 32% below its 52-week high of Rs 451. Some of the damage came from a sector-wide scare. In February, when Anthropic launched an AI tool that finds flaws in software code, Kedia's cybersecurity holdings sold off, and Sattrix fell 5% that day. docs.title: 142.1% profit growth: Why Hindustan Zinc still trades near its 52-week low
docs.text: Hindustan Zinc benefited from higher average prices of silver and zinc in the September 2026 quarter, and the resulting highest-ever revenue from operations along with record net profit in the quarter. Hindustan Zinc is among the world’s leading integrated Zinc producers. In addition, it is also amongst the top 10 global silver producers. Here is an insight on the factors driving the company’s record financial performance. FE Stock Insights on WhatsApPGet instant alerts on high-conviction investment themes and fundamental deep dives—direct from Financial Express.Join now The Silver Engine: How 103% Price Surge Powered 43% of Segment Earnings Hindustan Zinc sold 173 tonnes of refined silver in the second quarter of FY27, a rise of 17% y-o-y. Of equal importance, in its results presentation, the company has highlighted an average international price of silver of $ 62.6 per ounce as compared to $ 39.4 an ounce, a rise of 59% y-o-y. Global silver prices grew in the quarter on account of ‘safe haven’ status for this precious metal amidst US government debt crossing a record $ 40 trillion coupled with no signs of easing in the Middle East crisis. In the local market, average spot silver prices were nearly Rs 2.4 lakh per kilogram as compared to Rs 1.18 lakh per kg a year ago, a rise of 103% y-o-y. Part of the rise in local silver prices can be attributed to higher import duties imposed by the central government earlier this year. Silver prices had peaked at Rs 3.18 lakh in the third week of January, 2026. Hedging at $60/oz: Why Strategic Locks Cap Spot Upside Silver prices in the quarter were significantly higher on a y-o-y basis. However, in its annual report for FY26, Hindustan Zinc has highlighted that as part of its risk management framework, it undertakes strategic hedging for a portion of its annual production, within policy limits, to support greater predictability of revenues, EBITDA, and cash flows, and to mitigate adverse price movements. In line with this practice, the company hedged 59 tonnes of silver at an average price of $ 60 per troy ounce. The above position is intended to provide protection against price volatility, the company has highlighted. Hindustan Zinc sold 627 tonnes of silver in FY26. Depending on the commodity derivatives Hindustan Zinc has entered into, the company will leverage the upturn in silver prices, and it may not fully realise the rise in silver prices right away. Strong silver prices coupled with a rise in refined silver sold helped Hindustan Zinc’s silver division revenues rise 140.8% y-o-y to Rs 4,111 crore in the quarter. Also, segment profit of the silver business grew 146.5% y-o-y to Rs 3,609 crore in the quarter. However, it made up 43.1% of total segment profit of Rs 8,365 crore in the quarter. Core Industrial Base: Zinc Operating Profit Surges 120.8% on LME Rebound The company’s refined zinc sales were 214,000 tonnes in the quarter, a rise of 6% y-o-y. The company is the world’s leading integrated zinc producer. Importantly, the average LME price was $ 3,825 per tonne in the quarter, a rise of 35% y-o-y. Demand for zinc on a global basis is being driven by electric vehicles, construction galvanizing and infrastructure expansion. Also, refined lead sales were 51,000 tonnes in the quarter, a rise of 14% y-o-y. However, the average LME price of $ 1,857 per tonne, was 6% lower on a y-o-y basis. Demand for lead is driven globally by lead acid batteries for auto sector and data centre UPS back-up, amongst others. However, strong performance of the key zinc business helped revenues of this division rise 59.5% y-o-y to Rs 10,414 crore. Segment profit of this division also grew 120.8% y-o-y to Rs 4,720 crore. Strong performance of the silver and zinc division helped the company’s consolidated revenue from operations rise 76.5% y-o-y to Rs 15,093 crore in the quarter, and net profit also rose 142.1% y-o-y to Rs 6,412 crore. The RoE Asymmetry: What Hindustan Zinc’s 76.6% Return Masked Against Peers Hindustan Zinc has a consolidated return on equity (RoE) of an impressive 76.6%, according to Screener.in. Other leading non-ferrous players like Hindalco Industries has a 13% consolidated RoE. docs.title: Sunil Singhania’s 3 new SME bets: One is already up 189% from his entry
docs.text: Sunil Singhania's Fresh SME Stocks: Three Bets, Three Very Different Results Singhania is no stranger to big money. He spent about 15 years at Reliance Mutual Fund, now Nippon India Mutual Fund, where he rose to chief investment officer for equities, before leaving in 2018 to set up Abakkus Asset Manager. Abakkus now runs alternative funds, portfolio management services and a mutual fund. In September 2026 it filed draft papers with SEBI for its own IPO, which makes it one of the few money managers in India preparing to list on the market it invests in. Singhania has been on a what we can call a buying spree. Its recent moves into 5 stocks has caught investor attention. A few days earlier, he bought BEML betting on India’s bullet train aspirations. No wonder search interest in Sunil Singhania's portfolio tends to spike each time a filing shows him in a new name. SME stocks pull even harder, because the companies are small and the moves can be violent. Put the two together and you get a crowd of retail buyers asking one question. Should I follow him in? All three stakes sit with the Abakkus Venture Opportunities Fund, an alternative investment fund. In two of the companies, Abakkus did not buy on the exchange at all. It took shares in the IPO anchor book before listing at prices no retail buyer can get today. In the third, it bought through a bulk deal months after listing. That difference in entry price is the whole story. It explains why one position has nearly tripled while another is roughly where it started. Let us take them one by one, starting with the biggest winner. #1 Poojaa Precision Engineering: The Aerospace Vendor Driving a 189% SME Stock Gain Incorporated in 1992, Poojaa Precision Engg makes aluminium die-cast and machined parts. These go into car and truck engines, electric vehicles and industrial machines, and it has more than 600 products. It recently won vendor approval for aerospace parts and sells to customers in Germany, the US, Italy and Switzerland. Abakkus came in through the anchor book on 27th July 2026 at the issue price of Rs 301. The shareholding filed with BSE at listing showed Abakkus Venture Opportunities Fund with 2.35%. It also showed a second big name. Mukul Agrawal held 5.12%, the largest non-promoter stake. The IPO was subscribed 259 times and listed on 4th August at Rs 470. It closed at Rs 869 on 19th October 2026, about 2.9 times the anchor price. At that price, a 2.35% stake would be worth about Rs 41 cr against a cost of roughly Rs 14 cr. Promoters hold 60.63% of a business now valued at Rs 1,733 cr. docs.title: Apollo Micro Systems’ group company commissions 9,000-tonne explosives plant in West Bengal
docs.text: Hyderabad-based Apollo Micro Systems said on Thursday that its group company IDL Explosives Limited has commissioned a new bulk explosives silo plant near Asansol in West Bengal. The facility, called the Bolkunda Silo Unit, has a capacity of 9,000 tonnes. Apollo Micro Systems inaugurates 9,000-tonne Bolkunda explosives plant The unit was inaugurated on Thursday by Baddam Karunakar Reddy, founder and managing director of Apollo Micro Systems, according to the filing. Senior leaders of IDL Explosives were present. Reddy and the leadership team later planted trees at the site, which the company described as a reflection of the Apollo Group's commitment to responsible operations. The plant is spread over 8.4 acres. ALSO READMapletree, CapitaLand front-runners for Pune warehousing facility Bolkunda silo plant to supply bulk explosives to coal mines The company said the unit is located in the Eastern Coal Belt and the Central Coal Belt. It will serve the mining operations of Eastern Coalfields and Central Coalfields, along with other customers in the region. The supply will be site-mixed bulk explosives. The company said the silo-based set-up allows emulsion matrix to be converted into explosives at the point of use. This reduces the amount of finished explosive that has to be transported, it said, and adds to safety across the supply chain. IDL Explosives expands plant network to service Coal India orders According to the filing, the Bolkunda unit adds to IDL Explosives' national network of bulk explosives plants and silos. The company said it also strengthens IDL's capacity to service long-term bulk explosives orders from Coal India subsidiaries. The shareholder communication said these orders were secured earlier this year. Apollo Micro Systems described the silo as another step in the Apollo Group's energetics growth plan. It said the aim is to bring IDL closer to its customers. ALSO READNavratri auto retail hits 11.23 lk units: Tata Motors, Maruti gear up for Diwali rush How bulk explosives silos support mining operations The company explained that silos in the bulk explosives business are installed close to mining sites. They hold emulsion matrix, which becomes an explosive only when it is used. Each new unit therefore adds delivery capacity and ties the supplier more closely to the customer's mining operations, the company said. IDL Explosives is described by Apollo as the energetics platform of the group and one of the oldest names in commercial explosives in India. It manufactures packaged and bulk explosives for mining and infrastructure. The company also says IDL anchors the group's plans in defence energetics. About Apollo Micro Systems Apollo Micro Systems is a Hyderabad-headquartered developer and manufacturer of defence electronics and electro-mechanical solutions. Its products are meant for land, air, sea and space applications. Its customers include the Defence Research and Development Organisation, the Indian Armed Forces and defence public sector undertakings. Together with its group company IDL Explosives, the company says it is building domestic capability across weapon electronics, complete weapon systems and defence energetics. Apollo Micro Systems share price today Apollo Micro Systems’ share price decreased by 1.96% as of intraday on October 22. The company’s share price decreased 4.76% in the past month. However, Apollo Micro Systems’ share price increased 34.23% in the last year.

docs.title: Govt bond yields hit 7.45%: An opportunity for retirees or a warning sign?
docs.text: For someone nearing retirement, a government bond yield of 7.45% may look like an opportunity to secure a steady income for the years ahead. But there is a catch. The same rise in yields that makes fresh investments more attractive can reduce the market value of bonds already held in a retirement portfolio. For retirees who depend on their savings to meet monthly expenses, getting the balance right between income, safety and liquidity matters more than chasing a higher return. The yield on India's 10-year benchmark government bond rose to 7.45% on October 22, its highest level in three and a half years. Higher oil prices and global market cues have added to concerns about inflation and the future direction of interest rates. The move comes after a period of sustained pressure on government bonds, with the Reserve Bank of India raising its repo rate by 25 basis points in October and signalling a tighter policy approach. For retirement investors, the question is not simply whether a 7.45% yield is attractive. It is whether to lock in these yields now, wait for rates to rise further or stay invested in existing bonds and debt mutual funds despite short-term losses. The answer depends largely on when the money will be needed and whether the investor can hold the investment until maturity. Why are government bond yields rising? Three factors are putting pressure on Indian bond yields: rising oil prices, concerns about inflation and the direction of interest rates in India and other major economies. Crude oil is particularly important for India because the country imports a large share of its oil requirements. When oil prices rise, the cost of imports can increase. This can put pressure on inflation, the rupee and the government's finances. If inflation remains elevated, the RBI may have less room to cut interest rates and could keep monetary policy tight for longer. Retail inflation rose to 5.54% in September 2026 from 4.83% in August. Food inflation also climbed to 7.74%, adding to concerns about the cost of living. These figures strengthen the case for watching inflation closely while assessing the direction of bond yields. Kaustubh Sule, head of fixed income at Groww Mutual Fund, identifies global oil prices, the below-normal monsoon and its potential impact on food inflation, and the interest-rate gap between India and major developed economies as key factors driving the market. He also points to rising borrowing by governments and companies in advanced economies. When these borrowers need to raise large amounts of money, they can push up the cost of borrowing across global markets, including emerging economies such as India. Bond yields also respond to expectations about future interest rates. If investors expect rates to rise or remain high, they may demand higher yields before committing money to longer-term bonds. The RBI's October policy decision has added to this pressure. The central bank raised the repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.5% and shifted its stance to calibrated tightening. This has made investors more cautious about assuming that interest rates will fall soon. ALSO READHow to Build a More Resilient Fixed Income Portfolio Why rising US bond yields matter for India India's bond market does not operate in isolation. Developments in the US and other major economies can influence the returns global investors demand from Indian bonds. US Treasury bonds are closely watched because they are considered a benchmark for global borrowing costs. When US Treasury yields rise, investors can earn higher returns on dollar-denominated government debt. This can make Indian bonds less attractive on a relative basis, particularly when investors also have to account for currency movements and risk. Global bond markets have been under pressure in recent weeks. A report published by JPMorgan on October 19 noted that yields on major government bonds had climbed to multi-decade highs amid elevated energy prices, sticky inflation and expectations that interest rates could remain higher for longer. The US 10-year Treasury yield has also moved sharply higher. For India, the impact can come through several channels. Higher US yields can encourage global investors to reassess their exposure to emerging-market debt. If demand for Indian government bonds weakens, their prices may fall and their yields may rise. Higher global yields can also limit the RBI's flexibility. If the gap between Indian and US interest rates narrows, the relative attraction of Indian assets may weaken, although currency expectations and other factors also influence investment flows. For retirement investors, this global connection matters because even government bonds with very low credit risk can experience price volatility. The government's ability to repay its debt and the market value of that debt are two different things. Three risks retirees should watch before investing A higher government bond yield can be attractive, but retirees should consider three risks before increasing their allocation. 1. Inflation can reduce purchasing power Even when an investment offers a fixed return, the money may buy less in the future if prices rise. India's retail inflation reached 5.54% in September 2026. A 7.45% yield is higher than that inflation reading, but this is only a rough comparison. The actual return after inflation will depend on future price increases, taxes and the yield earned over the holding period. 2. Interest rates may rise further Higher oil prices, pressure on the rupee and persistent inflation could keep borrowing costs elevated. If market yields rise further, long-duration bonds may lose more value before stabilising. Investors who may need to sell early should be particularly careful. 3. Credit quality and liquidity still matter Government securities have very low credit risk, but corporate bonds carry different levels of risk depending on the issuer. docs.title: India’s warship boom has a catch: Why Goldman Sachs is betting against Mazagon Dock, GRSE
docs.text: Goldman Sachs has assigned 'Sell' ratings to the two key shipbuilder stocks, warning that the completion of major programmes, delays in fresh orders and easing margin benefits could weigh on earnings through FY29. Goldman Sachs has initiated coverage of both Mazagon Dock Shipbuilders and Garden Reach Shipbuilders & Engineers (GRSE), setting 12-month target prices of Rs 1,855 for Mazagon Dock and Rs 1,515 for GRSE. The brokerage expects EBITDA at the two shipbuilders to decline at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 19.3% between FY26 and FY29, compared with projected growth of 26% for the other aerospace and defence companies under its coverage. The report's concern is not a lack of long-term demand for Indian warships. Rather, Goldman Sachs argues that the timing of new contract awards, the pace of current project completions and the companies' valuations leave them exposed to a period of weaker earnings. Goldman Sachs writes: “India accounts for less than 1% of the global shipbuilding market, with defense and military vessels accounting for almost 75% of the domestic market vs. 22% globally.” Goldman Sachs on both shipbuilders: Orders must catch up with deliveries Goldman Sachs says both companies are approaching the end of major delivery programmes, with their trailing book-to-bill ratios at cyclical lows. The ratio compares new orders received with revenue recognised, indicating whether incoming business is replacing completed work. The brokerage puts the trailing book-to-bill ratio at 1.37 times for Mazagon Dock and 1.81 times for GRSE. It argues that high revenue in the current phase partly reflects the execution of older contracts rather than a continuing increase in the order pipeline. Goldman Sachs writes: “Consequently, trailing Book-to-Bill has fallen to cyclical lows (1.37x for MAZG; 1.81x for GRSE), signaling that current record revenues reflect peak billing on depleted backlogs rather than sustainable momentum.” The distinction is central to the brokerage's assessment. Shipbuilding contracts typically take years to move from tendering to execution and delivery. A company can report strong revenue while its order book declines, leaving a gap between the completion of current work and the start of new programmes. Goldman Sachs also says both companies trade at a premium to global shipbuilding peers on a market capitalisation-to-order book basis, despite having smaller order books and weaker near-term earnings prospects. It expects the earnings decline and uncertainty around fresh awards to constrain their valuations. Figures rounded where appropriate; FY29E denotes estimates. Mazagon Dock: Earnings could weaken before recovering Goldman Sachs expects Mazagon Dock's revenue to decline to Rs 11,678 crore in FY27 from Rs 13,006 crore in FY26, and further to Rs 10,642 crore in FY28. The brokerage forecasts a recovery to Rs 14,666 crore in FY29, but expects the intervening period to bring lower earnings. Its EBITDA estimates fall to Rs 3,189 crore in FY27 and Rs 2,998 crore in FY28 from Rs 3,405 crore in FY26, before rising to Rs 3,903 crore in FY29. Earnings per share are projected to decline to Rs 54.97 in FY28 from Rs 64.04 in FY26, then recover to Rs 70.56 in FY29. Goldman Sachs writes: “We initiate coverage of Mazagon Dock Shipbuilders (MAZG) with a Sell rating and 12m TP of INR 1,855” The brokerage identifies a declining order book and the fading contribution from early deliveries and reversals of liquidated-damages provisions as risks to near-term earnings. Mazagon Dock's order book fell to Rs 18,200 crore at the end of Q1 FY27 from around Rs 50,000 crore in FY21, according to Goldman Sachs. The report also examines the contribution of liquidated-damages provision reversals to reported profitability. Such reversals accounted for around 13% to 28% of additional EBITDA during FY24-FY26, while a reversal of Rs 304 crore in FY24 related to two P-75 submarines. Goldman Sachs expects Mazagon Dock's EBITDA margin to be around 11% in FY27. Its concern is that earnings could lose some of the support provided by these earlier benefits as the company works through its current programme cycle. Mazagon Dock share price performance GRSE:Next Generation Corvette award is a key variable GRSE faces a similar challenge, with Goldman Sachs identifying uncertainty over the Next Generation Corvette (NGC) contract as a key risk. Delays in the award could leave the company with fewer new projects ready to replace programmes approaching completion. The brokerage forecasts GRSE's revenue to rise to Rs 7,980 crore in FY27 and Rs 8,470 crore in FY28 from Rs 7,000 crore in FY26, before falling to Rs 5,060 crore in FY29. EBITDA is expected to increase to Rs 1,310 crore in FY27, then decline to Rs 1,250 crore in FY28 and Rs 1,080 crore in FY29. Earnings per share are forecast to rise to Rs 81.01 in FY27 from Rs 65.29 in FY26, before declining to Rs 77.23 in FY28 and Rs 65.73 in FY29. Goldman Sachs says margins could also come under pressure as the benefit from early vessel deliveries fades. docs.title: HAL to BEL: Nifty Defence Index drops 6% – Is the Dip a Buy or warning sign for investors?
docs.text: After steadily rising for several months this year, the Nifty India Defence index has lost some momentum in the last three months. The recent consolidation signals investors’ worries about weakness in order executions, after the sector had rallied on strong capital expenditure. The index has gained over 14% so far in 2026. However, it has declined over 6% in the last three months. Some of the worst hit names in these three months include Cochin Shipyard, which has declined nearly 15%, Bharat Dynamics has lost around 16%, Mazagon Dock Shipbuilders has lost 17%, and Bharat Electronics, which has fallen over 10%. Stocks like Garden Reach Shipbuilders & Engineers and Data Patterns (India) have declined nearly 25% and 18%, respectively. Structural Downturn or Temporary Consolidation? “The recent weakness looks more like consolidation after a strong run rather than a change in the structural story. Defence stocks have delivered substantial returns this year, and after such a move, profit-taking is natural,” said Rahul Sharma, Director, Head - Technical & Derivative Research at JM Financial Services. ALSO READ4x oil production target by FY30: An under-the-radar smallcap betting on bigger profits Sharma terms the current phase as “expectation reset” rather than a “fundamental deterioration.” Some of the other analysts Financial Express spoke to also echoed a similar sentiment. Pankaj Kumar, VP Fundamental Research at Kotak Neo said, “After a period of strong outperformance, defence stocks have corrected in line with the broader market. The sector had previously rallied on the back of strong defence spending, healthy order prospects and heightened geopolitical uncertainty.” The recent weakness in the sector reflects a combination of slower order conversions and a correction in elevated expectations. Delays in the awarding of major programmes such as the Quick Reaction Surface-to-Air Missile, Project-75(I) have created uncertainty around the timing of future growth. “Defence procurement is inherently lengthy, and approvals do not immediately translate into signed contracts or revenues. Following the sector’s strong rally, demanding valuations had also left limited room for disappointment, prompting profit booking,” said Santosh Yellapu, Research Analyst at Anand Rathi Institutional Equities. Yellapu added that investors are increasingly scrutinising delivery schedules, supply-chain constraints, and the conversion of order books into earnings and cash flows. The Nifty defence index is transitioning from an aggressive bull phase into a period of “prolonged consolidation”, according to Ankit Soni, Research Analyst at Mirae Asset Sharekhan. The root cause of the anxiety is the growing realisation of an acute weakness in execution across the sector. “The sector has always got a premium in the war times which is now fading away. Geopolitical tensions and military conflicts globally acted as a major tailwind for defence stocks over the last two years. As immediate war-related enthusiasm cooled, the market started demanding evidence of earnings delivery rather than simply buying the geopolitical narrative,” Soni said. Buying Opportunity? The recent downturn in the sector does present an opportunity to buy. However, analysts cautioned that investors should not be aggressively bullish and rather take a staggered approach to accumulate quality businesses. Kotak’s Kumar said, “We believe the recent correction provides an opportunity to selectively accumulate defence stocks with a long-term perspective, supported by rising geopolitical tension, accelerating modernisation programs and an expanding export opportunity.” JM Financial’s Sharma said the long-term opportunity in the defence sector remains compelling, driven by India’s increasing focus on indigenous defence manufacturing, import substitution, higher domestic procurement, and exports. However, valuations across several defence companies already reflect a significant part of this optimism. “Therefore, the correction should be used to accumulate quality businesses in a staggered manner, rather than treating every decline as a buying opportunity. My approach would be simple: buy businesses where earnings growth can justify valuations, not stocks merely because they have corrected,” Sharma said. ALSO READIndian IT stocks rally 12% in a week – Is the turnaround sustainable? Anand Rathi Institutional Equities’ Yellapu also said investors should selectively buy, with a three-to-five year horizon. “Valuations remain demanding in parts of the sector and need to be assessed against achievable earnings growth, execution capabilities and cash generation. We would favour staggered accumulation in companies with differentiated technologies, credible management, healthy balance sheets and clear order visibility,” he added. Preferred Bets Kotak’s Kumar said the correction has improved risk-reward for select stocks, especially those exposed to a strong pipeline of large programmes. Kumar prefers Bharat Electronics and Hindustan Aeronautics. Mirae Asset’s Soni also picked Bharat Electronics and HAL as the preferred stocks. “BEL is widely preferred for its exceptional capital efficiency, boasting a Return on Capital Employed (RoCE) of approximately 35% to 36.5%. Because its electronics and radar systems are platform-agnostic (used across ships, aircraft, and ground vehicles), it faces significantly lower supply chain concentration risk than platform builders,” Soni said. docs.title: 4x oil production target by FY30: An under-the-radar smallcap betting on bigger profits
docs.text: For years, Asian Energy Services made money by helping other companies look for oil and gas. It provided the technical services needed to understand what lay beneath the ground, develop fields and keep energy infrastructure running. It did not need to own the oil to earn from the business. Now, it wants a bigger share of the economics. The company is expanding from technical services into oil and gas production, adding an international services business and building out its mineral infrastructure operations. The attraction is straightforward. A company that provides services, earns fees for the work it performs. But a company that owns a producing oilfield can also benefit from the hydrocarbons it extracts. FE Stock Insights on WhatsApPGet instant alerts on high-conviction investment themes and fundamental deep dives—direct from Financial Express.Join now Asian Energy Services 1-Year Share Price Chart Source: Screener.in That second business comes with a different set of risks. Producing oil requires capital, output can disappoint and commodity prices can change the economics of a project. The question is whether Asian Energy Services can turn this shift into a more profitable business, rather than simply a larger one. From finding oil to producing it Asian Energy Services has more than three decades of experience in specialist services such as seismic surveys. These surveys help energy companies understand what lies beneath the ground before deciding where to drill. The company later expanded into engineering, procurement and construction (EPC), operations and maintenance (O&M), integrated field development and mineral infrastructure. The next step came in September 2025, when Asian Energy Services moved forward with the proposed merger of Oilmax Energy. The National Company Law Tribunal sanctioned the merger on 29 September 2026 and the company received the certified order on 15 October 2026. The merger brings producing and developing oil and gas assets into the business, extending its role from providing services to energy companies to earning directly from oil production. It brings producing and developing oil and gas assets into the group, moving Asian Energy Services beyond simply earning fees for providing services. It can now also benefit from the oil and gas produced from these assets. ALSO READ4 Small-Cap Stocks with Rising Promoter Stakes for Two Consecutive Quarters The businesses could complement one another. Seismic surveys help identify resources, field development prepares them for production and maintenance keeps facilities running. Oilmax adds the opportunity to earn from the hydrocarbons themselves, while mineral infrastructure provides a separate source of business linked to mining and material handling. More importantly, Oilmax could change the economics of the company. Oil production can generate higher margins and faster cash flows than project-based services. If production increases as planned, it could lift the group’s profitability and reduce its dependence on the services business. But that benefit is not automatic. Developing oilfields requires capital and production can fall short of expectations. The real test is whether Asian Energy Services can turn its broader business into higher margins, stronger cash flows and better returns for shareholders. Revenue has taken off. Margins have gone the other way The recent numbers show that the expansion is changing the company’s growth. Consolidated revenue from operations rose 70.1% in FY26. EBITDA grew at roughly half the rate of sales and the EBITDA margin fell from approximately 15.6% to 12.5%. In other words, the company generated substantially more revenue but retained a smaller share of each rupee as operating earnings. Kuiper, an international energy-services business, was acquired in 2025 and has been included in Asian Energy Services’ consolidated results since September that year. Some of the reported growth reflects adding a business that was not included in the previous year’s full-year consolidated figures. The company also reported an exceptional charge of Rs 9.4 crore in FY26, including acquisition-related costs and a write-off. Reported profit and profit adjusted for exceptional items should therefore be kept separate when assessing its performance. The June quarter of FY27 showed faster growth, but the margin question remained. Consolidated revenue increased 135% year on year. Yet the EBITDA margin declined to 8.1% from 10.5% in the corresponding quarter a year earlier. The company has cited the volatile Middle East operating environment, while the mix of contracts also influences quarterly margins. These factors may explain part of the pressure, but investors need to see the improvement in profitability in the reported numbers. Faster revenue growth is useful only if more of that revenue eventually reaches the bottom line and generates cash. Why the Rs 1,754 Crore Order Book is Only Half the Story The standalone order book stands at about Rs 1,754 crore. Oil and gas services account for 60%, with mineral services making up the rest. The figure excludes Kuiper and Oilmax, as well as covering third-party contracts for the standalone business. Asian Energy Services’ Rs 1,754 Crore Order Book: Where the Business Stands Source: Company Presentation Management has also identified an active bidding pipeline of Rs 3,000 crore to Rs 4,000 crore. These are opportunities, not confirmed orders. Winning them is one thing; delivering them at profitable margins is another. The order book, therefore, tells only part of the story. Projects can be delayed, costs can rise and customer payments can take time. Growth creates value only when the company earns a reasonable return on the work it undertakes. docs.title: Stocks to watch on Oct 23: Swiggy, HPCL, Sagility, Colgate, and more
docs.text: The earnings for the second quarter of financial year 2027 (Q2FY27) are in full swing. The shares of the following companies will remain in focus on October 23, after they announced their quarterly results after the markets closed on Thursday. On Thursday, the Sensex fell 460.30 points, or 0.62%, to settle at 73,249.39. Similarly, the Nifty 50 declined 123.70 points, or 0.54%, to close at 22,687.65. Swiggy Swiggy has reported a net loss of Rs 922 crore in Q2FY27. The company had posted a loss of Rs 1,092 crore in Q2FY26 and a loss of Rs 791 crore in Q1FY27. Swiggy’s revenue stood at Rs 7,571 crore in Q2FY27, up 36.14% from Rs 5,561 crore reported in Q2FY26. On a sequential basis, Swiggy’s revenue rose 11.14% quarter-on-quarter (QoQ). ALSO READ142.1% profit growth: Why Hindustan Zinc still trades near its 52-week low Cyient IT firm Cyient posted a year-on-year decline of nearly 5% in its Q2 FY27 net profit, which was reported at Rs 121.40 crore, down from Rs 127.50 crore reported in the same quarter last year. The company’s bottom line contracted, driven by margin pressure and high investments towards its R&D vertical. Cyient also announced its first interim dividend of Rs 12 per share for FY27. Cyient’s revenue from contracts with customers stood at Rs 2,235 crore, rising over 25% YoY from Rs 1,718 crore. On a sequential basis, its revenue expanded around 8% from Rs 2,076 crore reported in the trailing quarter, while the tech firm’s net profit jumped nearly 17% from Rs 104 crore reported in Q1 FY27. HPCL Navratna PSU Hindustan Petroleum Corporation’s (HPCL) net profit fell 6% year-on-year to Rs 3,625 crore in Q2 FY27 against Rs 3,859 crore reported in the year-ago period. On a sequential basis, the company bounced back into profit against a net loss of Rs 12,264 crore reported in the trailing quarter. The oil marketing company’s consolidated revenue from operations for the quarter ended September stood at Rs 1.39 lakh crore, advancing nearly 29% YoY from Rs 1.10 lakh crore reported in the same quarter last year. On a sequential basis, HPCL’s topline contracted 4% from Rs 1.45 lakh crore reported in the trailing quarter. Colgate Palmolive (India) Colgate reported a net profit of Rs 341.5 crore for the September quarter, up 4% YoY from Rs 328 crore a year ago. Its revenue rose 12% to Rs 1,705.7 crore from Rs 1,520 crore a year ago. The company’s EBITDA rose nearly 2% to Rs 474 crore from Rs 465 crore in the year ago quarter. Colgate’s EBITDA margin contracted to 28% from 31% a year earlier. Sagility Sagility reported a net profit of Rs 284 crore for the September quarter, up 13% YoY from Rs 251 crore. Its revenue grew around 23% to Rs 2,032 crore and EBITDA was up 23% at Rs 512 crore. However, the company’s EBITDA margin was unchanged YoY at 25% for the quarter. Adani Total Gas Adani Total Gas reported a net profit of Rs 167 crore for the quarter, up 3% from Rs 162 crore reported a year ago. The company’s revenue from operations rose 34% YoY to Rs 1,936 crore. Adani Total’s EBITDA increased 11% to Rs 326 crore for the quarter, from Rs 293 crore in the year-ago quarter.. However, EBITDA margin contracted to 16.8% from 20.3% a year earlier. docs.title: Rs 760 cr orders, 157% profit growth: An under-the-radar smallcap rides the global grid boom
docs.text: India’s power equipment sector is seeing sustained demand as the country expands and modernises its electricity grid. Demand is not limited to India. It extends globally, including the US and Europe. The latest Q2FY27 earnings offer an early glimpse of how companies are performing as investments in power infrastructure gather pace. Macro Drivers: How the ₹9.15 Lakh Crore NEP Fuels Grid Equipment Demand Government initiatives such as the Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme (RDSS), with an outlay of ₹3.0 lakh crore, aim to improve the efficiency and reliability of distribution networks. With only around 22% of sanctioned transformers installed so far, implementation could create further demand for distribution equipment. At the transmission level, the National Electricity Plan (NEP) projects an investment outlay of around ₹ 9 lakh crore through 2032 to support grid expansion and modernisation. The NEP also envisages expanding the transmission network to 6.48 lakh circuit kilometres by 2032 and increasing transformer capacity to around 2,345 GVA. Global demand is adding another layer of opportunity. Over 4 crore power transformers in the US are ageing and could trigger a multi-decade replacement cycle. So demand for transformers and parts is not just strong in India but surging globally. And several companies are tapping into this opportunity. Today, we focus on a small-cap stock that is tapping into this opportunity. It recorded a 157% growth in profits in the recently ended quarter. And, to give a glimpse into the future, it has seen its order book nearly double. Other than this company, we also take a look at a relatively well-known stock from this sector. This company too has logged 100%+ profit growth and is firing all engines. FE Stock Insights on WhatsApPGet instant alerts on high-conviction investment themes and fundamental deep dives—direct from Financial Express.Join now #1 Yash Highvoltage: High-Voltage Bushings Eye Global Expansion and Growth Yash Highvoltage manufactures condenser-grade high-voltage, high-current transformer bushings. It is India's only independent manufacturer of condenser-grade transformer bushings and is among fewer than 12 independent producers globally. The company has installed over 50,000 transformer bushings to date. The company produces Resin-Impregnated Paper (RIP), Oil-Impregnated Paper (OIP), resin-impregnated synthetic and High-Current transformer bushings (voltage ratings spanning 24 kV to 245 kV and current ratings up to 25,000 A). The company also provides wall-through bushings, retrofit solutions, and on-site testing/repair services. Backlog Runways: Inside Yash’s ₹760-Crore Domestic and Export Pipeline Domestic sales account for 86%, exports 6% and Retrofit & Services 8%. The company’s order book has almost doubled to ₹760+ crore as of September 30, from ₹400 crore in the same period last year. This provides revenue visibility of about 15-24 months. Note that the company reports half-yearly earnings ending September and March of every year. The company sold 35.6% more bushings, reaching 4,000 in H1FY27 compared to 2,950 in H1FY26. To capture higher margins, the company has shifted toward higher-voltage-class bushings, which command higher realisation per unit. This transition was led by RIP bushings, which contributed 86% of total revenue by value in H1FY27. Operating Leverage: Why Margins Rose 480 Bps on 95% Revenue Growth Revenue grew 95% year-on-year to ₹194.5 crore in H1FY27, allowing fixed overheads to be absorbed over a much larger volume base. This expanded EBITDA (Earnings Before Interest, Tax, Depreciation, and Amortisation) margins from 23.3% to 28.1% and net profit margins from 13.7% to 18.6%. Consequently, net profit surged 157% to ₹36.2 crore. The Cash Conversion Cycle improved to 63 days (compared to 81 days at the end of FY26) due to tighter operational controls. Operating cash flow surged to ₹45.2 crore in H1FY27, compared to ₹4.8 crore in H1FY26. The company holds a net cash position of ₹95 crore as of September 30, 2026, with a near debt-free Debt-to-Equity ratio of 0.03. Management highlighted a favourable environment driven by global shortages of high-voltage transformer bushings. The company benefits from both the Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme, under which only around 22% of sanctioned transformers have been installed so far, and the ₹9.15 lakh crore National Electricity Plan (NEP) transmission outlay through 2032. US Grid Replacement Cycle: Yash’s Roadmap to ₹1,000 Crore Revenue Management notes that ageing electrical grid infrastructure worldwide, including over 4 crore US power transformers past their design life, is triggering a multi-decade replacement cycle. Renewable energy integration and data centre power demand require new step-up and power transformers, each needing 5 to 7 bushings. To capitalise on this opportunity, the company is commissioning a greenfield plant in H2FY27. This plant will add 6,000 units of annual capacity and increase the voltage rating to 550 kV. This paves the way for peak combined revenue of ₹1,000 crore. It is also in the trial phase to localise core manufacturing of RIP/RIS bushings which were previously 95%+ imported. Global Export Playbook: Commercialising 550 kV Bushings via US Tie-Ups Yash has also established its dedicated sales and marketing subsidiary, Yash HV USA, to establish direct relationships with US utilities, transformer OEMs, and procurement engineers. Yash HV USA signed a 36-month representation agreement with key US sales agencies, including Ensales Electrical Associates, Inc., Gateway Power Sales and EV Solutions LLC. Yash already maintains an active US order book, with order delivery schedules typically spanning 6 to 15 months. Current exports to North America consist primarily of OIP bushings. Once the greenfield plant becomes operational, Yash will begin exporting dry-type RIP/RIS bushings directly to North American and European markets for the first time. Yas

docs.title: Dixon vs Cyient DLM: Why JP Morgan prefers 1 stock after 27% EMS correction
docs.text: India’s electronics manufacturing services (EMS) stocks have come under pressure after earnings disappointments exposed differences in growth expectations, returns on capital and valuations. In its 20 October 2026 research report, JP Morgan argues that companies in this capital-intensive sector cannot be valued on earnings growth alone. The brokerage continues to prefer Dixon Technologies and Amber Enterprises India, remains ‘Neutral’ on Kaynes Technology, and rates Syrma SGS Technology, Avalon Technologies and Cyient DLM ‘Underweight’. Cyient DLM’s earnings miss triggers a sharp correction According to JP Morgan, Indian EMS stocks fell between 6% and 22% over the month preceding its report, compared with a 2% decline in the Nifty. Among the sector’s year-to-date outperformers, Cyient DLM fell 22%, Avalon Technologies declined 17%, and Syrma SGS Technology lost 10%. JP Morgan noted that Cyient DLM suffered a sharper fall after its second-quarter results missed expectations on both revenue and margins, while the company also reduced its FY27 margin guidance. The stock dropped 27% over two sessions, even as the Nifty remained broadly flat. The brokerage linked the size of the correction to the expectations already built into the share price. Cyient DLM had risen 148% year to date before announcing its results, while the Nifty was down 12%. JP Morgan’s 12% reduction in its FY27 earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) estimate was followed by a stock-price correction of more than twice that percentage, which the brokerage attributed to heightened expectations. JP Morgan also questioned the valuation gap between Cyient DLM and Dixon. Cyient DLM had been trading at a premium despite lower expected earnings growth and ROCE. The brokerage considered that premium unjustified given the difference in the companies’ growth and capital-return profiles. ALSO READNSE India to Moneyview: $24 billion IPO lock-in expiry in 101 stocks by next January Why JP Morgan believes ROCE belongs in the valuation JP Morgan’s central argument is that earnings growth must be considered alongside the returns a company generates on its invested capital. EMS businesses require substantial capital expenditure and can carry high net working capital (NWC), making the efficiency with which they use capital an important part of their valuation. JP Morgan stated in its report: “Though P/E multiples are driven by earnings growth in the EMS sector, we believe one has to bake the ROCEs into the multiples as well, given the capex-intensive and high-NWC nature of the sector. Hence, we believe that among companies with comparable earnings growth, the premium multiple should be deserved by the ones having higher ROCEs.” The brokerage argues that companies with comparable earnings growth should not automatically command similar price-to-earnings (P/E) multiples. In JP Morgan’s assessment, a business generating stronger returns on capital has a better basis for earning a premium valuation than one delivering similar growth with lower capital efficiency. JP Morgan also identifies three conditions under which the market is likely to pay greater attention to ROCE: an earnings miss, slower growth and persistently high working-capital requirements that weigh on free cash flow (FCF). The brokerage’s view is that when these conditions arise, a company’s ability to convert reported earnings into cash becomes more important to its valuation. JP Morgan draws a lesson from the previous EMS correction JP Morgan points to the sector’s previous correction as an example of how market attention can turn from growth to cash generation and capital efficiency. The brokerage wrote: “In our view, the market will start looking at ROCEs once (1) there is a miss on earnings, (2) growth slows down, and (3) NWC remains high, thereby negatively impacting FCF. This scenario played out late last year when EMS stocks had rallied from Jan-Oct ’25 but then Kaynes missed revenue growth expectations and its NWC days also expanded, driving negative cash flows; this shifted the market focus to BS/CF and ROCEs of these businesses, driving a correction in other EMS names also.” According to JP Morgan, Kaynes’ revenue growth shortfall and rising working-capital days were accompanied by negative cash flows, prompting greater attention to balance sheets, cash flows and returns on capital across the sector. The brokerage connects that period with the correction in other EMS stocks, rather than treating the earnings performance of each company in isolation. ALSO READSunil Singhania’s 3 new SME bets: One is already up 189% from his entry JP Morgan applies the same framework to Cyient DLM. When results fall short of expectations, a stock’s previous gains and valuation can leave less room for disappointment. The brokerage argues that earnings growth alone may not sustain a premium multiple when capital efficiency and cash generation do not provide comparable support. JP Morgan names Dixon its preferred EMS stock Dixon Technologies remains JP Morgan’s top pick in the sector, followed by Amber Enterprises. The brokerage compares expected earnings growth between FY26 and FY28 with forward P/E multiples and expected ROCE to assess the relative valuations of the companies under its coverage. JP Morgan stated: “Dixon stands out, given its higher earnings growth and ROCE and, hence, deserves a premium multiple, in our view.” In JP Morgan’s assessment, Dixon’s combination of higher earnings growth and stronger ROCE supports its premium valuation. The brokerage’s argument is not that the cheapest stock should always be preferred, but that a premium multiple should be supported by the quality of a company’s growth and the returns it generates on capital. Amber Enterprises is JP Morgan’s other preferred stock. Both companies carry ‘Overweight’ ratings, reflecting the brokerage’s preference for their combination of earnings growth, capital efficiency and valuati

docs.title: Vodka vs whisky: Why Jefferies sees a new growth opportunity for Radico Khaitan
docs.text: Think about the last house party you attended. Was it whisky or a vodka cocktail? More often than not, it is a cocktail. According to Jefferies, white spirits are “India’s fastest-growing spirits category”. Their volumes grew above 20% a year over calendar years 2021 to 2025. The wider market for Indian Made Foreign Liquor (IMFL) grew only about 6% a year. For investors tracking the sector, Radico Khaitan is a stock to watch. According to a Jefferies report, white spirits are gaining ground faster than the broader market for Indian-made foreign liquor (IMFL). Radico’s Magic Moments vodka brand has been a key driver of this shift, although rising competition could influence how the market develops. Why is vodka gaining ground in India? India’s white spirits segment, which includes vodka and gin, has grown at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of more than 20% between calendar years 21-25, compared with around 6% for the overall IMFL market, according to Jefferies. white spirits make up around 6% of Indian spirits sales. Globally, the share is 20-25%. According to the global investment bank report, white spirits volumes could rise from around 18 million cases currently to 50 million cases over the medium term. ALSO READFrom ₹16 lakh to ₹60,000 crore: How this teetotaller family built a liquor empire What is changing consumer preferences? Vodka’s relatively light taste and ability to mix with other beverages have helped it gain popularity in cocktails, house parties and bars. Younger adult consumers and women are among the groups contributing to changing consumption patterns, while cocktail culture is spreading beyond major cities. Flavours are another important factor. According to Jefferies, “Flavoured vodka now accounts for ~65% of category volumes.” Companies can introduce new flavours more quickly than they can change aged whisky products, giving vodka makers more opportunities to experiment and attract customers. Why does Radico Khaitan stand out? Radico Khaitan has built its position in the category through Magic Moments and its range of premium offerings. According to Jefferies, the company delivered a 21% premium and above (P&A) volume CAGR between FY20-21 and FY25-26, compared with 8% for United Spirits and 13% for Allied Blenders and Distillers. The report also noted that Radico’s vodka saliency increased from 16% in FY20-21 to 22% in FY25-26. It expects the figure to cross 25% in FY26-27. However, competitors are investing in their own products. United Spirits has increased its focus on Smirnoff, while Allied Blenders and Distillers plans to enter the deluxe vodka category. ALSO READDixon vs Cyient DLM: Why JP Morgan prefers 1 stock after 27% EMS correction Can white spirits improve profitability? Vodka does not require the lengthy ageing process associated with many whiskies. Jefferies estimates that white spirits profitability could be 1.5-2 times that of whisky. For Radico Khaitan, the key factors to watch are continued demand for Magic Moments, premium product sales and its ability to defend market share as rivals expand.
